speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I ask permission to draw the attention of the House to a statement that appeared in the Toronto ' News ' of Saturday last, given on the authority of a government official, with reference to the snowstorm reported to have occurred in certain parts of western Canada about a week ago.

warmer there lasit night than in Toronto. The damage by snow and frost must have been considerable. A week ago to-day it snowed steadily all day and all night at Regina.
Now, the assertion that it snowed steadily all day and all night at Regina, 1 believe to he entirely unfounded, and I am surprised that a government official should give publicity to such a mistaken assertion. The information which I have received by letter from Regina since the date of the storm, which unfortunately did prevail over a limited area in the western part of Manitoba and the eastern edge of the Territories, is to the effect that the Regina district did not suffer much damage from the storm. maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: And that less than ten per cent of the grain would be threshed.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: And as my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) says that less than ten per cent of the grain would be threshed. That is an exaggeration that is purely and simply ridiculous. As a matter of fact from the best information obtainable, I believe that the snow-storm did not affect possibly more than one-fifth of the grain growing area of western Canada. The storm originated in the United States and drifted northward. It was very severe in Colorado and Nebraska. It travelled over Wyoming, South Dakota, North Dakota and Montana and it seemed to peter out, so to speak, when it arrived in Manitoba. There was a limited area in Manitoba of which, I think, Virden was about the centre where there was a considerable fall of snow. My information is that even in that area the damage is not likely to be very severe. No person can state with any authority yet just what the damage will be but I do not believe that within the area visited by the snow-storm the damage will exceed ten per cent and taking the country as a whole I do not believe it will amount to as much as five per cent at the greatest. I move the adjournment of the House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question which has been brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) is certainly a very important one and I think correct information should be given to the country as soon as possible in opposition to the reports which have been sent out, so as to acquaint the public with the fact that the harm done to the crops of the North-west lias not been such as the reports would indi- . cate. The information that I have received from my own constituency, where, I understand, the storm was possibly the heaviest, is that the effect of it has been very slight indeed. I have reports from twenty-five or twenty-six different places in my own constituency and in nearly every one of these places my information is that the loss will be scarcely more than three per cent, and in that case the evidence is not very certain. Tn some places they had started threshing three days after the storm. A great many people upon reading the report of a snowstorm in that country are under the impression that it is a most disastrous thing. It would if the crops were standing. Most of the crops have been cut and the great bulk of them are now stacked. Possibly not more than ten per cent of the crop is still standing in the stook and even if a snow-storm does overtake the crop in that condition the effect is not as serious upon it as a heavy fall of rain because the snow will not penetrate the stacks or stooks to as great an extent as the rain will. speechtext:
I now beg to move :
That section 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
(3) Notwithstanding anything in this Act, or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained, on behalf of the Dominion of Canada unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have entered into an .agreement with His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall covenant and agree as follows :
(a.) That the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, so long as the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall hold the common stock of the said Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to the amount of $24,900,000, shall perform. fulfil and carry out according to the true intent and meaning thereof, all the provisions of this Act and all the covenants, stipulations and conditions in the said agreement, which according to the terms thereof ought to be performed, fulfilled or carried out by the said Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
In submitting this amendment to the Com mittee a week ago, I pointed out that under the form of this agreement the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada is not bound to the Crown at all, hut the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is hound to the Crown by some very important stipulations in the agreement contained. I also pointed out that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, by reason of holding practically the whole of the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, could at all times, and would at all times, absolutely control the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Under these conditions, and particularly in view of the fact that it has been stated by the ex-Minister of Railways that these two companies, according to his view of the agreement, are practically one and the same company ; in view of the fact that that interpretation of the contract lias been expressly assented to by the Minister of Finance in adopting the very forcible ex-

pressious used by the ex-Minisber of Railways ; in view of the fact that we have from the Prime Minister himself, and several member's of the cabinet, the express and absolute statement that these two companies are, for the purposes of this great enterprise, practically one and the same company, there seems to be no good reason why not only the Grand Trunk Pacific shall become bound to the Crown in these important stipulations, but that the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself shall so become bound to the Crown. The stipulations to which I refer are undoubtedly of a very important character. I do not pretend to deal exhaustively with this agreement at the present moment, but among the most important of these stipulations are those contained in sections 41, 42, 43 and 45. Clause 41 of the agreement is as follows :
At ail times during the terms of the said lease, the company shall continuously and efficiently operate both divisions of ithe said railway, giving due and sufficient service for the accommodation of all traffic to the satisfaction of the government.
I am not aware that the government has any security for the fulfilment of that agreement beyond the security which will be contained in the second mortgage upon the rolling stock which is to be appropriated to the eastern division. The lolling stock amounting to $5,000,000 for the eastern division is to be mortgaged to the government by a charge which will be subsequent to that contained in the mortgage upon the said property to secure the bonds guaranteed by the government. I am putting aside for the moment the question as to whether or not it will be necessary, under the terms of this contract, that the Grand Trunk Company should be absolutely possessed of the rolling stock, or whether it is possible for that company to satisfy the conditions of the contract by merely obtaining rolling stock under a lease or rental agreement. Get me assume, for the purpose of this argument, that it is necessary that the company shall be absolutely possessed, in its own right, of the *entire interest of the rolling stock of the eastern division. The rental of the eastern division is secured in the same way. This mortgage is to secure, not only the efficient operation of the railway, hut also the rental. I say the government do not seem to have a very important security for either the efficient operation of the railway or the rental, even if they adopt the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice as to the character of the interest which the company must acquire in the rolling stock for the eastern division. I have not any accurate computation of the rental, but I suppose it might perhaps amount to $2,500,000 a year. This has been suggested by some of my hon. friends beside me. That rental is to extend over a period of forty years ; and, as security for that rental, which might amount during that time 371*
to $100,000,000, the government have only a second mortgage on $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock. So that, even for the rental, apart from the efficient operation of the road, you have not a very important security under the terms of this agreement. Then, for the efficient operation of the road, you have to rely upon the same security, and, of course, I always desire to he understood as not forgetting the fact that you have the covenant, the bald covenant, of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the same thing. But inasmuch as the property of that company is to be covered by three mortgages, and as branch lines which are expected to be built will undoubtedly be covered by mortgages which will provide for the construction of those branch lines, you have not very much security for the efficient operation of the eastern division of this railway, or indeed for the operation of the western division, although we would have probably less concern about that than about the eastern division, because, humanly speaking, we might consider that there would be no very great question about the operation of the western division after the road was once constructed. That condition of affairs would seem to indicate that it would be a very proper thing that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, controlling, as it will absolutely, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, by reason of holding practically all the common stock, should bind itself to the terms of this agreement, and among others, to the terms of section 41, by which the company has undertaken the efficient operation of both divisions of the railway.
Section 42 of the agreement provides as follows :-
I.t is hereby 'declared and agreed (between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express 'purpose of encouraging the development oh- Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through-rats on expert traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
In some remarks which I made to the House at a former stage of this Bill, I expressed the opinion that an agreement couched in that language might not be a very effective guarantee to the government or the country that traffic would be carried between Canadian inland points and Canadian ports. I .expressed my reasons to the House at that time, and I shall not repeat them ; and what I say now is, of course, subject to the remarks I then made. But

the majority of this House, the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches and their followers, did not take the same view of the effectiveness of that provision that I entertained ; and, therefore', I am bound, so far as any effect will be produced by the terms of that provision, to see that it shall be binding, not only on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, which is to be a mere form, but on the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself, which shall control at all times and during a period of fifty years the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It is for that reason, among others, that I urge that the government should make all the stipulations in this contract which are binding on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company also binding on the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is in one sense making this contract with the government through the medium of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I have already pointed out that that is a very advantageous position for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to occupy, because, while absolutely controlling the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, while able to dictate its policy through holding practically all the common stock, it is at the same time not subject to any of the stipulations- contained iii this agreement, because the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself is not a party to this agreement. Now, if ht is desirable-and we are bound to so assume under present conditions-that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should make this covenant with the government, is it not infinitely more desirable that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should itself make the same covenant ? The Grand Trunk Railway Company will build the railway through the west, we must assume, at a very early day. It will be anxious to get access to the wheat fields of the west and to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway for that enormous traffic in grain and other articles which is developing so rapidly in that great country. Well, during that period, we are led to believe, by statements made by ministers of the Crown which I have quoted to the House on previous occasions, that during a considerable period the eastern division of this railway will not have been constructed. So that we shall have the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, controlled absolutely by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, running its lines into the north-western country for several years before the eastern division of this railway shall have been completed. What follows from that ? It follows that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, controlling the policy of the Grank Trunk Pacific Company, will be able to compete in the most effective manner for all the traffic gathered by the Grand Trupk Pacific Company in the west. The Grand Trunk Railway Company will have more to do with the bringing of that traffic to the eastern sea-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
ports than any other corporation or influence in Canada ; and during that period at least-nay, during the Whole period of forty or fifty years during which this arrangement shall be carried out-is it not infinitely more important that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should he bound by a stipulation of this kind than the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ? I have adverted on a former occasion to the danger pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), who explained to this House that it would be a very simple thing for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to make connection with Winnipeg from Chicago, and bring out the traffic which it would pick up in the western country over those lines running into the United States, and carry it to its great terminals at Portland, where it has expended, I understand, about $20,000,000, according to a statement made in tl(is House by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. I pointed out the other day that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce seemed to think that was a rather imminent possibility, and that there was not one word or line in this contract which prevents the Grand Trunk Railway Company doing that very thing the day after this agreement was signed. My hon. friend the Prime Minister, in answering my observations a week ago, took the ground that there was nothing in the danger which I have pointed out, following in that regard the language of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who, he said, was on the whole favourable to the terms of this agreement.
Get me point out to my hon. friends on the treasury benches that this is not very much of an answer. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is able to point out a danger which exists, on account of the Grand Trunk Railway having connections between Winnipeg and Chicago. Have I not the right to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the other gentlemen on the treasury benches to show me that in the agreement or in this Bill, they have safeguarded in any way the people of this country from that danger. And is not that danger one which will be imminent during the period of seven years which members of the government admit will elapse before the eastern division of this railway can be completed ? Ministers of the Crown have taken it absolutely for granted that a very considerable period of time will elapse between the date when the Grand Trunk Railway through the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, will be picking up traffic in the west and the date of the completion of the eastern division of the railway. It is obvious that there is a great deal in the opinion they have expressed in that regard. We know that a railway through a prairie country presents no great difficulties or obstacles ; we know also, that very little, if anything, has been ascertained as to the difficulties to be en-

countered in constructing the eastern division, from Moncton to the city of Winnipeg, and it seems to be agreed, by common consent in this House and in the country, that the period of time to which I have referred will elapse between the dates I have mentioned.
Let me point out another section of the contract which is important in that regard, section 43, which reads :
The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely,-the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Looking at sections 42 and 43, let us consider the possibility of the Grand Trunk Railway, by means of its agents and officials, whom it will undoubtedly send into the western country for the purpose of securing traffic, forwarding traffic not along Canadian routes exclusively, but over its own rrnad and to the city of Portland. Is there any line in the contract which will prevent the Grand Trunk Railway from doing that ? There is obviously not a syllable in the contract that will prevent the Grand Trunk Railway from adopting that course because that company is not a party to this agreement.
Let us look at section 45, which reads :
The company shall arrange for and provide, either by purchase, charter or otherwise, shipping connections upon both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, .sufficient ill tonnage and in number of sailings to take care of and transport all lbs traffic, both inward and outward, at such ocean ports within Canada, upon the said line of railway, or upon the line of the Intercolonial Railway, as may bo agreed upon from .time to time, and the company shall not divert, or, so far as it can lawfully prevent permit to be diverted, to ports outside of Canada any traffic which it can lawfully influence or control, upon the ground that there is not a sufficient amount of shipping to transport such traffic from or to such Canadian ocean ports.
Is there any reason, if this agreement is to be carried out in good faith by the Grand Trunk Railway with the Crown, why the Grand Trunk Railway Company, controlling absolutely the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific and holding all its common stock, should not hind itself by an agreement under which it shall guarantee to the government and the people of this country that these stipulations to which I have referred shall be carried out in good faith by the Grand Trunk Railway. It may be that there is some stipulation included within the terms of this contract to which reasonable objection might be taken by the Grand Trunk Railway. If so it can he excluded from the terms of my amendment, but, up to the present time, I have not been made aware of any such stipulations which the Grand Trunk Railway Company ought not to make good. I therefore move that
section 7 be amended by adding thereto the section which I have just read.

speechtext: When the hon. member (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was addressing the House before recess he moved an amendment, the general purport of which, I think I am correct in saying, was to require that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was to require that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was to become responsible for all the undertakings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of Canada. We object to that, for the simple reason that it is not in the contract, and, not only is it not in tile contract, but it is not quite consistent with the contract. I suppose that in any transaction between two parties, the government being one, if the other party to the contract was to pay $5, it would be very desirable, that he should pay $10. We would admit that it was very desirable, but, if it was not in the contract we could not exact the other $5. What my hon. friend asks is additional security, and, from this point of view it is very desirable. But it is uot in the contract, and therefore, we are not in a position to ask it. I suppose there is danger of confusion of the public mind between these two companies, the Grand Trunk Company the old company- and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. We think it is advisable that they should be closely united, and, as far as possible identical. We have called attention to this feature of this bargain-I know that I myself have done so-by saying that these two companies become practically one; and what we mean by that is explained by the discussion which took place on the terms of the agreement. The old Grand Trunk Company agrees to do certain things. These things are in themselves important. They are of sufficient importance, we think, to call attention to them and dwell upon them. But it does not follow that, because they did agree to do certain things which are important and which we value, we must call upon them to do something else which they have uot agreed to do and which it would be unreasonable for us to ask them to undertake. The Grand Trunk Company as the hon. leader of the opposition says, are uot parties to this contract. It is proposed, however, that they shall be parties to It, as their officials have assured us that they were prepared to do certain things

Verbal- that is all that can be had at this stage. They have said that the Grand Trunk Company is prepared to do certain things. We proceed, in the contract and the Bill, on the

assumption! that they will do these things. If they will not do these things, of course we shall not do our part of the arrangement. The one follows the other. But the Grand Trunk Company proper-the old Grand Trunk Company-can only do these things in a proper and official way, and the time has not yet come for that. However, we have no doubt that they will do them. Now, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has suggested, as respects certain things, that it is well to stipulate that we shall only do our part when they have done the things set out in the Bill

speechtext:
Yes, when they have bound themselves to do them-the hon. gentleman's suggestion is correct. We have accepted that because it is in line with our interpretation. But, as the present amendment goes further and asks us to require them to do some things which they have not bound themselves to do and which they have not assured us they will do, and which I suppose they have no intention of doing, we cannot agree to it. They have undertaken to do certain things, and we have the assurance of their officials, which, I presume, will be carried out in regular official form as required by /his Act, that they will do these things. We nave assurance that they will take and hold certain common stock of the company. We think that important. For this reason-that the stock will not be allowed to go into the market and pass into the hands of other persons, and possibly at a later stage, be treated, in the fixing of the freight rates, as capital at a fictitious value. We think it important, for several reasons, that the Grand Trunk should take and hold that stock and not dispose of it. Instead of that being merely a privilege given to the Grand Trunk Company, we think it is a privilege which carries certain responsibilities of value to the country. Therefore we insist that they shall acquii'e, take and hold that stock. We think the country is in a better position to have its interest protected if the Grand Trunk take and hold that stock than if they were to put it on the stock market as in the case of other stocks. They having assured us that they will do that, we shall be right, before we do anything, before we give a guarantee or accept responsibility, in requiring them formally, in their capacity as a corporation, to do that thing, and that is secured by the amendment to which we have already agreed. Then, the Grand Trunk Company have assured us through their officials that they will do another thing, that is, to guarantee the bonds of the new company to the extent of one quarter of the cost of the company's road, and more than one quarter, if necessary, inasmuch as the government only guarantees three-quarters not exceeding a limited sum; the balance Hon. whether one-quarter or more than one-quarter must be provided by the Grand Trunk Company by its guarantee and on its responsibility.

We have no assurance of officials that is not expressed in the words .of the contract. It was fully understood, I think, between the Grand Trunk and the government that our interpretation of the contract and theirs is the same. However, without reviving a previous discussion, I may say that this is what the Act requires, and that they have assured us that they are prepared to do what the Act requires. We get, then, from the old Grand Trunk Company two things which we regard as important. We get an undertaking to acquire, take and hold this common stock-and we think that as between having the Grand Trunk take and hold it and a different policy, one of floating the stock on the money market to be speculated in, their acceptance of this condition is a matter of substantial value. In the second place, we have their undertaking-which, at present, is only an assurance, but, we believe, will be implemented by their solemn covenant as required-to guarantee the bonds for the remaining portion of the western division. These two things are important, very important, so important that they identify the Grand Trunk Company with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in the closest possible manner. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) now comes forward and says that the Grand Trunk Company must not only acquire this stock and hold it as we propose, must not only guarantee the bonds for the remaining quarter, or possibly more than quarter of the money required for the completion of the western road, but they must, over and above that, become guarantors for all the obligations of the new company. That is not in the contract and not in the Bill, and to insert it now as proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition would be to insert something not in the contract. We have no right to ask the Grand Trunk to do it. I meed not tell my hon. friend, as a man of experience in these things, that, while we would have a perfect right in case of obscurity, something not clear, to put in a clause defending that in a manner we all understood, yet we have no right to insert something /entirely inconsistent with the contract itself. And it would be inconsistent with the requirements of the contract to put in these new conditions which would oblige them to become guarantors in a manner and to an extent not contemplated by the agreement. In the case of one company purchasing the stock of another company-and, I believe, there are such cases

in railway transactions-I do not understand that the purchasing company becomes the guarantor of the obligations of the other; it takes the stock and becomes responsible to the extent of the stock. Whatever obligations follow the purchase of the stock the purchasing company would assume, but they would mot assume all the obligations of the other company. These are reasons why, I think, it would not be fair and equitable to ask the Grand Trunk Company, the old company, to accept this new and broad general responsibility. We claim that we do get from the old Grand Trunk Company two things of importance to which I have referred-one that they should take and hold the stock and thus identify themselves closely with the undertaking, and the second that they should become the guarantors of the bonds to the extent of one-quarter or possibly more of the balance required for the building of the western division. In these two things we have obligations on the part of the Grand Trunk which we think are of value; and, if additional obligations on the part of the old Grand Trunk Company are asked, as in the amendment of my hon. friend, all we can say is that they are not in the contract and we have no right to demand them.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext:
This is just as much in the contract as is the matter dealt with in the amendment which has been accepted by the government. My hon. friend does not seem to realize that. There was a provision in this contract which did not bind the Grand Trunk Company, but did bind the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, that the Grand Trunk Company should guarantee the bonds of the company for the balance required for the construction of the western division. That was not binding upon the Grand Trunk Company, the covenant Itself was not made by the Grand Trunk Company ; and the government accepted my amendment declaring that this agreement should not be binding upon the government until the Grand Trunk Company itself shall by agreement have bound itself to the government that that provision should be carried out. The matters I brought to the attention of the committee just before recess are precisely of the same character. We find certain stipulations here in this agreement which are of the utmost possible importance from the standpoint of the government and of the people of this country. Those stipulations are not binding upon the Grand Trunk Company, because it is not a party to the contract ; that company, nevertheless, controls the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ; and one of the arguments that my hon. friend made to the House on this point was in these words-and I can cite a dozen other illustrations of the same language made use of by members of the government during the progress of this debate :
What w-e regard as a very strong feature of the project is that it is to be carried out by practically the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada.
But are you carrying out this feature when one of the most important provisions of the agreement is not binding upon the Grand Trunk Company at all, but is binding only upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, especially when the danger, if danger there be in this respect is danger to be apprehended, not from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, but from the Grand Trunk Company itself ? Where does the danger lie? Does it lie in any possible future action of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, considered apart from the Grand Trunk Company, if you can so consider it ? No the danger lies in the fact that the Grand Trunk Company has important connections in the United States of America, connections which have been pointed out by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of the Interior, and other members of the government. That is where the danger lies. Nevertheless the safeguards contained in this measure, such as they are, are safeguards, not against any action of that kind on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but against action on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, where It is less to be feared than in the other quarter. My hon. friend went on to say further in the same connection :
We have required that the Grand Trunk Railway shall not only be behind this undertaking, but in it and of it.
How is the Grand Trunk Company in any proper sense of the term in this contract and of it, if it is not bound by these very important stipulations to which I have called attention ? I do not realize exactly the attitude of my hon. friends. Here are stipulations against carrying tlie freight to ports other than Canadian ports ; here is a railway company with which the government has some understanding, the Grand Trunk Company ; here is that company having its terminus in the United States, a terminus upon which there has been expended some $20,000,000, as we are led to believe by the Minister of the Interior and by the Minister of Finance, and not one single line of this agreement has any effect whatever upon the Grand Trunk Company as a corporation distinct from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. The agreement was drawn in- rather a remarkable way, it seems to me, iu the first instance. The ordinary course of preparing an agreement of that kind would be to make it between the Crown of the first part, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company of the second part and the Grand Trunk Company of the third part, and by providing stipulations in the agreement that will bind not only the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, but the Grand Trunk Company itself, stipulations which have been devised in the public interest for the purpose of securing the car-

riage of Canadian traffic within Canadian channels. But that is not the shape in which the measure is presented to the House ; it is presented in the shape of a contract between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company alone ; and although by the scope of that contract you are to give the* Grand Trunk Company absolute command of the future policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific, you do not find in that contract from first to last one single line, one single stipulation, which is intended to be binding upon the Grand Trunk Company. When my hon. friend has to meet that difficulty, after it has been pointed out by his own colleague, what is his answer ? His answer is that what we propose is not within the terms of the contract. True, it is not within the terms of the contract, but it should have been within the terms of the contract in the first instance, and it is because it is not within the terms of that contract that we are now asking for such an amendment to this Bill as will make those stipulations binding upon the Grand Trunk Company ns well as upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
What possible difference in principle is there between accepting the amendment which we are now suggesting and the amendment which the government accepted a moment ago, regarding a covenant by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company that something should be done by the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; the government accepted that amendment, and under the Bill as it will now pass, the government is relieved from the stipulations on its part until the Grand Trunk Company shall have entered into a covenant with regard to guaranteeing these bonds. But so far as the remaining stipulations to which I called attention are concerned, the position remains exactly as it was before. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company is bound, the Grand Trunk Company is not bound, and as it controls absolutely the future policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, it is not in the slightest degree debarred from using every Influence within its power to send that western traffic over its own road and to its own American port. There cannot be any doubt about that. Yet the Minister of Finance thinks that is not a matter to be guarded against in the public interest. But why should it not be guarded against in the public interest? He says you cannot force the Grand Trunk Company to accept it. It is true you cannot foi'ce the Grand Trunk Company to accept it but you can say that this aid is dependent upon the Grand Trunk Company accepting it, and you can say that the many millions of public money of this country which are proposed to be devoted to that enterprise, shall not be given until these obligations are binding, not only upon the Grand Trunk Pacific, but upon the Grand Trunk Company itself.

THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: Trunk Railway Company is at its back in the sense of being its backer, according to sporting parlance, that is one story, but if the Grand Trunk Railway is so far at its back that it is out of sight and out of reach, that is another story, and when hon. gentlemen opposite ask the country to support a certain scheme because that scheme has this backing of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, surely we are not asking too much, though recognizing the value of that support, in asking that it should be a genuine backing. If this contract is to be placed under the control of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if it is to have all the advantages of the contract made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, surely it ought to be prepared to assume some of their responsibilities. I think the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition will improve the contract. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I think, will adlmit that we have a right, not to amend the contract in the sense of amending it as it is signed and which binds either party, but amending it in the sense that we will only agree to it if such and such terms are adopted and then submit the contract or the amendments to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company for their acceptance.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext:
on the part of the Grand Trunk people in making this contract. I do not want to say anything against any corporation in this country, but I wiil say, that the Grand Trunk has always been regarded as a bankrupt body. I am not saying that offensively; I hope some day the country will be big enough to afford them sufficient traffic to enable them to pay interest on their securities. It has been known for 40 years that the Grand Trunk has defaulted on its securities. At one time it defaulted on its first and second securities, and then it paid interest on the second, and a while ago it paid interest on the third ; but they have not paid a cent of interest on two out of the five classes of securities they hold. I hope, in the interests of Canada, that they may succeed in paying interest on these last two classes of their securities : but surely it is not going to be said, that a company that cannot pay interest on all its securities is a company that will give credit and character to a new enterprise. You recollect reading in the newspapers one morning this summer, that the Grand Trunk president in London was approached by his shareholders who said :	This new scheme
will involve our system in enormous expenditure, and as we are just beginning to make money, do not mix us up with such an enormous new enterprise as this, and in reply to that, that president of the Grand Trunk Company in London said :	The old
Grand Trunk will not be responsible for a single dollar in this new scheme. It is to carry out that pledge of the president of the Grand Trunk to his shareholders that we have this ingenious patehed-up scheme, presented to us to-day. The Grand Trunk do not intend to commit themselves to the expenditure of a single dollar, but they want to get into the great wheat fields of the west ; they want a feeder for their old Grand Trunk system ; they want to take the wheat and other freight of this country, to Portland, where the whole energy of their system is centred. They arei not satisfied with using Canada as a highway ; they are not satisfied with taking the whole trade of Ontario to Portland now, but they want to add to it all the trade of the west, and to divert the trade of the west to the United States. When the Finance Minister gets down to Nova Scotia, he will find that the people fear that this Grand Trunk system will ruin the prospect of the maritime provinces for ever in getting the trade of the west. And now when it is proposed by the leader of the opposition to take some steps to hold this Grand Trunk Railway Company in some way under our control, or the control of the courts, the Minister of Finance gets up and says : We have made a binding contract. He ought to be anxious that we should point out to him where we can strengthen this contract. We say that the Grand Trunk ought not to have all this financial aid without us having good security that in the end we shall get what we
bargained for, but the Minister of Finance endeavours to make it sure that we shall have no security. He votes down our amendments, when, on the contrary, he ought ..to say to us : We thank you for your amendment; have you any more in the same direction ?
We are not captious critics ; we are not here to oppose this government; we are here to strengthen and aid them in making a contract in the highest interests of Canada. I venture to say that this agreement will result in the greatest misfortune to Canada. I am sure that it will result in the greatest misfortune to the maritime provinces. Nova 'Scotia, which for thirty years had been hoping to get the export trade of Canada, will, if this agreement is completed, be farther away from the goal than she was at the Inception of confederation. Sir Charles Tupper and Mr. Howe, and all the leading men of Nova Scotia, implanted the idea in the bosom of the people of that province that Halifax was to be the wharf of Canada. We want to fulfil that promise. I understood, when this Bill was introduced, that the government were attempting to fulfil that promise, because the Prime Minister went over the history of the efforts of previous governments to bring trade to the maritime provinces. He cited the efforts of Sir Charles Tupper to build railways across New Brunswick for that purpose. That was one of the bases of this proposition. And yet when the leader of the opposition points out that there is a fatal defect in this scheme, in that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is mot bound by it, and that the' Atlantic terminus of that railway is already at Portland, the reasonable induction is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will proceed to use their old system and exploit it in such a way as to take the business to Portland. When it is pointed out that we have no hold on the Grand 'Trunk Company, and that we can get a hold upon them only by compelling them to hold the stock in this Grand Trunk Pacific Company at its face value, the Minister of Finance' says : That is 'quite true, but we do not want to make any corrections of that kind, because the Grand Trunk Company do not want them, Mr. Cox does not want them, and the other people behind this agreement do not want them. But the people of Canada want them. Look at the enormous sums of money which we are going to vote for this scheme. It will probably take $200,000,000 ; and if carried out on the splendid lines proposed by the hon. member for North Norfolk, it wall take $300,000,000 and perhaps $400,000,000. He is a magnificent exploiter of railways. I like liis ideas, and if we laid down a true railway in the interests of Canada, I would not care if it cost $300,000,000 or $400,000,000. But the proposal to spend even $10,000,000 on a rotten scheme of this kind has my most strenuous opposition. We have

in Canada the routes to control the trade, not only of this continent, but of the world ; and if we bad not been the sleepiest people on God's earth, we would have had the trade of the east, and Canada would have been a great nation to-day. Those great statesmen from Ontario, McMullen and Gibson, who adorned this House, did what ? When we want to have a great national discussion, some lion, gentlemen get tired and go out ; but when McMullen and Gibson were exploiting the great question whether the Speaker of this House should get his napkins washed once a week or not, or whether Sir Charles Tapper should have a separate wine glass for each course which he offered to his guests in England, they occupied months to settle that vital question. If the Liberal party had shut these little fellows up when they wasted the time of this parliament in discussing such questions, and had undertaken at that time to debate this great [transportation question, they would have added something to the upbuilding of Canada. But down to this day the Liberal party have never added one brick to this great edifice of Canada. They have attempted to undermine it, to blow it up, to destroy it, but they have not added one brick to the edifice down to this moment. This is the first attempt of the Liberal party to add one brick to the edifice, and what is it ? Is it a gold brick, or a miserable brick of paper, such as confidence men hand to honest men for their good, solid money ? I suppose, on behalf of my province, as this debate goes on. to show that each clause of it is a complete sell. We were told in the corridors that the government were bringing down such a measure that no man from the maritime provinces would dare to vote against it. They attempted to gold-brick the members of this House by saying that their measure was so perfect that we dare not criticise it. I venture to say fjiat no measure ever introduced into this parliament will meet such determined opposition in the maritime provinces as this scheme. Not because we do not want railways ; we want dozens of railways ; but because, as a national railway, it fails in every particular. If the government had treated with the Grand Trunk Railway Company and had compelled them to own a line from ocean to ocean, there would be something to be said for if ; but when they split this scheme into two divisions, east and west of Winnipeg, and get the dark shadow of the Grand Trunk behind it, they ruin it for ever. This is a scheme devised by the Grand Trunk Company. The Minister of Justice and the government of Canada had nothing to do with it. It' was matured in London by splendid railway lawyers, probably looked over in New York by railway sharks there, and manipulated by some other lawyers in this country, and then handed over to the government; and they werei innocent enough to accept it without understanding Mr. GOURLEY.
it. The shadow of Cox so darkened the Privy Council chamber when they were considering it that not a man of them could see a line of the contract.

speechtext:
My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) spoke rather disparagingly of the obligations assumed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company under this contract, because, as he said, that company was worthless. I cannot say that I agree with him in that statement, because, after all, when he considers the contract, he must realize that before anything is done to give effect to this contract, it is necessary for this company to deposit $5,000,000 with the government, and furthermore, he realizes-because I have heard him admit it in this House-that under this contract the government are legally not under any obligation to endorse the bonds of the company to the extent of a farthing until such time as the whole enterprise is completed from Winnipeg to the coast. Now, it seems to me that no company that was absolutely worthless, that had not some strong financial backing, would be in a position to put up five million dollars and to undertake to build a road extending from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. The hon. leader of the opposition put the question in this form : What difference is there in principle between the amendment that we accepted this morning and the amendment we are now discussing ? I find a vast difference between the two. The first amendment provides that before the government can be called upon to endorse any bonds in aid of the construe-

tion of this road, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall see to it that the Grand Trunk Railway Company enters into a contract by which they shall bind themselves to guarantee a second issue of bonds. That was the first amendment, and that, in my humble opinion, simply gave effect to the condition of the contract. I argued, some days ago, that the obligation to subscribe the stock and to guarantee the second issue of bonds was a condition precedent to the government obligation to guarantee the first issue of bonds. The hon. leader of the opposition thought that that was not quite clear, and, in fact, went so far as to say that it was not a condition precedent. I argued that it was, and in order to set the matter at rest, we have adopted this amendment. What is the amendment which is suggested now ? Not that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall enter into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company to have something done that is provided for by the agreement, but that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall enter into an undertaking for the due performance of all the conditions of the Bill and of the contract. Now, there is no such provision in the contract. I submit that the Grand TrunkRailway Company-not according to the letter of the contract, but according to its-true intent and meaning-will be practically-obliged to see to it that all those conditions-of the contract to which the hon. the leader of the opposition referred this morning, are-carried out. My hon. friend said, 1'or instance, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be in a position to divert traffic,-as was said by the right hon. Minister of. Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) by Chicago and thence through the-United States and by its line through Ontario to Portland. But my hon. friend (Mr.-Borden) did not construe the words used-by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce as I did. The Minister of Trade and-Commerce said that if this line was not built by North Bay, then this diversion might occur, but that the building of this line from Winnipeg to Quebec, with a branch line down to North Bay would make that diversion impossible. Now, I said that the spirit, if not the letter, of this contract is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should carry out the conditions of this contract. Take, for instance, the obligation to operate the road. I assume-for this can be only a matter of opinion-that it is a matter of the most vital importance for the Grand Trunk Railway to have a connection with western Canada for the whole of its Ontario system. It seems to me that it is a matter of vital importance that that road, which at present has its western Canadian terminus at North Bay, should have access to the west, should have connection through Canadian territory Between its lines in Ontario and western Canada, and without the
construction of this road, how is it possible to secure such connection ?

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: Without the construction of what road ?

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext:
Without the construction of this road east from Winnipeg to Quebec, with branch lines to North Bay and to Port Arthur. How is it possible to utilize its magnificent system in Ontario so far as western Canadian trade is concerned, unless it reaches western Canada by North Bay and Winnipeg ? I say it is a matter of absolute necessity for the Grand Trunk Railway to have an entrance for its magnificent Ontario system into the west, and that an entrance is provided by this road. If they do not utilize this road in its entirety, would any government be justified in permitting them to use it partially, to use it merely to connect at North Bay, and not to use the section to Moncton and the maritime provinces ? To my judgment, it is inconceivable that any government would do anything of the kind. Look at the preamble of the contract, which provides for the construction of the railway, and which was agreed to by both parties of the contract. The preamble provides :
For the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, to be operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion of Canada from ocean to ocean and wholly within Canadian territory.
That is the preamble of the contract, that is the statement of the common intention of both parties to the agreement, in which both concur, that they are to build a railway through Canadian territory from ocean to ocean. Then, you have got, moreover, this provision in section 42, which reads :
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties ito this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
The agreement there provides that the condition upon which the whole of this aid is granted! is. that the goods of the west shall have an outlet through Canadian channels. To say that under these circumstances we cannot enforce that contract against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and against any party interested in this road seems to me to be impossible to conceive. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not say that the letter of this agreement provides for anything to be done by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The amendment that we have accepted does not oblige the Grand Trunk Railway to do anything. What is in the amendment is, that we are not subject to do certain things for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, until the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway has secured this-contract from the Grand Trunk Railway Company. All we

can do is to rely upon the conditions which will exist after this road is brought into operation, when the Grand Trunk Railway, of necessity, must use this road for the purposes intended. That is the case, as I understand it, and under such conditions it is impossible to accept this amendment, because it would imply au obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to get the Grand Trunk Railway Company to guarantee the fulfilment of all the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway under this contract. All I can say is, that there was never any expectation that there would be such an obligation, except so far as such an obligation may result from the general terms of the contract.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext:
As the present discussion is largely a legal discussion I shall endeavour to confine it myself to matters which are of a legal or quasi-legal character. We have a definite, square proposition made by the leader of the opposition in the amendment which he proposes. It is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall, with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, be liable for the fulfilment of the contract and stipulations entered into with the government. A good deal has been said by the Finance Minister which can be very easily admitted. We admit, of course, that the mere fact that one company purchases the stock of another comiiany does not involve the responsibility for debt. But there is. a long distance between that and the circumstances of this ease ; and it becomes more emphasized when we consider the nature of this Bill as originally introduced and the speeches made by supporters of the government and members of the cabinet throughout the whole discussion. What we have had impressed upon us, both when this Bill was introduced and on every occasion when it has been discussed is this-that we are getting the security of the old Grand Trunk Railway Company. That has been repeated in various forms and it has been made of significance in this country-that we were not getting a contract with a paper company, but we were getting a contract with a company having large connections in Canada, and that these two systems would work together In harmony to the great advantage of this country. The hon. Minister of Justice, who has just spoken, emphasizes this view of the matter. He says that in this railway project it was found to be necessary, in the interests of Canada, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should have an extension west from North Bay. What the reason is-if this is the main object-of having an extension east of North Bay is not very apparent. But I leave that point. If it was found necessary in the interest of Canada to have an extension of the Grand Trunk westward from North Bay, what is that but saying that, though nominally and on paper, the Grand Trunk Pacific is Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
entering into this enterprise, yet, in truth and in fact, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company only, are the parties constructing this line ? And can there be any doubt that they are to be beneficiaries in this matter, if we glance back at the whole of this transaction ? From the very first day it appeared in committee down through all the stages of the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, we have had here the representatives of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and practically of the Grand Trunk Railway Company alone. Now, the Minister of Finance made an important statement of fact, namely, that we have no assurance from the Grand Trunk Railway Company beyond what is expressed in the contract itself. We know, therefore, definitely, so far, what the Grand Trunk Railway Company propose to do. But, as I understand it, this does not, and should not end the matter. This is a provisional contract, placed before parliament for its approval. If it is a contract perfect in all its details and satisfactory to the people's representatives, well and good ; but it would be perfectly idle for us to debate the matter if the contract was to be accepted as a matter of course. We are here to find out whether this scheme is in the interest of Canada at all. Parliament has practically decided that point up to a certain stage. But, assuming it to be in any sense in the interest of Canada, it is for us to say whether, in its present shape, it shall or shall not become a completed contract ; and to that end we are discussing it. It is perfectly idle, in view of what the Minister of Finance has said-I say it with all deference to the Minister of Finance-for us to discuss the matter, if his view is to obtain that because a thing is in the contract, that is the end of it. We want to frame the provisions of this Bill in such a way that it shall control the contract so far as necessary in the interest of Canada. Now, I disagree-with the usual deference-with the proposition of the Minister of Finance that we have all the assurance from the Grand Trunk Railway Company that we possibly can have at this stage of the proceedings. It is perfectly clear to any one who will consider the matter, not only that we could have a different state of things before this committee, but that we ought to have a different state of things before this committee. Before this matter reached this stage at all, we should have had not only a contract signed by the parties to this contract; but if the Grand Trunk Railway Company was to stand as the sponger for this company, as was alleged at the initiation of this Bill, we should have bad a contract signed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company as well. Then we should not be met with, what I submit is somewhat captious, opposition by some members of this government. We have to treat it, however, as we have it. Now, this

project was launched as a great national scheme, as the solution of one of the greatest problems that have confronted the people of Canada, the great transportation problem. It was launched as the means by which we would secure the transportation of the products of the west through Canadian routes. That has been the burden of the speeches made by supporters of the government, and that was the strong plank upon which the right hon. gentleman who introduced this measure stood. And it was pointed out more than once-it was pointed out almost every day of the discussion-that if once we allowed that Canadian products of the west to find an outlet through American channels, it would be impossible, or next to impossible to win back that trade to Canada. Now, this is not a great national project. The only way you can secure that end is by securing identity of the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company with the interests of Canada. If you make it to their interest-and you can only do that by making it a matter of hard and fast contract-if you make it to their interest that the products of the Canadian west shall pass through Canadian ports, then you can to a certain extent, at all events, secure that desirable end, but, if you do not do that, this end can never be secured.
It has been pointed out, and I think the government must be impressed with the fact, although it was not expected at the time this contract was hurriedly entered into-it has been pointed out over and over again to the government that by reason of the fact that the western division of the railway is to be constructed before the eastern, there is a danger that the commerce of the west will drift over to the United States, and thence by the system of the Grand Trunk to Portland. You must therefore, by this contract-and this amendment will tend to secure that end- you must create a community of interest between Canada and the Grand Trunk Company. At present there is a hostility of interest between Canada and) the Grand Trunk. Their interest is to carry the products of the west, not by the long haul north of the Canadian lakes, but to drift it to the United States and carry it by way of their present American system. And not only is this amendment required, but more than this amendment is required in order to prevent that disastrous result. In the one case you may get some return for your money-I do not think you will get an adequate return for it-in the other case, if you allow the crops of the west and the commerce of the west to drift through the United States, instead of following a Canadian highway, to the national benefit of Canada, you will be promoting a national disaster. But that is not the only danger. I am addressing myself more particularly to the 42nd, 43rd and 45th clauses. As pointed out by the leader of the opposition, the 41st section is also involved in this matter of a national agreement; and greater even than the issues involved in the 41st section, is.the question of where our commerce shall drift, and whether this shall or shall not be a national highway. I want to point out that the danger of its drifting immediately through American channels is not the only danger. We are to have a branch railway to Port William or to Nepi-gon bay, and we are to have a branch railway to North Bay. So far as the working out of this scheme is concerned, it is not necessary to have a line from North Bay to Moncton. The Grand Trunk can tap this system at the branch running down to Port William, or to Nepigon bay, or to North Bay, and they can divert the traffic there, and there is no clause in this contract that will prevent it. What you have to get, if you are to secure in any degree the benefit of the results that were so glowingly pictured when this Bill was introduced, is to identify the Grand Trunk Railway closely with the contract, make them parties to the contract ; otherwise you will have the result that, although the paper company, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, is bound, the Grand Trunk Company, Che substantial parties behind the transaction, the men who are controlling the situation, the company which, we are told, is the security upon which this measure is launched, is not bound, and will be at liberty to do just what they please. Now, without saying anything harsh about the Grand Trunk Railway Company, I think the history of that company in the past as regards the shipment of its freights to Portland, has not been such as to inspire us with confidence that, unless you have them bound hard and fast, you will secure the end we desire. Now, it would be well for the government to take this matter into consideration : Is or is not the government willing, at this stage, to take steps which shall secure that measure of benefit to Canada which is the only excuse for introducing this measure at all ? Will they take the steps now, or will they simply refuse ? It is perfectly idle for the government to say that it is not in the contract, and because it is not in the contract it cannot be carried out. We are the persons who offer the terms upon which our railways shall be built. If we think fit, we can recall this measure from this company altogether. If we do that, we will find many capitalists in Canada and elsewhere ready to take it upon easier terms than you have offered to this company. But I do not assume that will happen. I say, all you have to do, and all that we are here for, is to say : A proposal has been made by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the Grand Trunk Company ; we want certain terms ; it is the duty of the government to exact every reasonable term. It is not the duty of the government to say : Oh, it is not in the

i
contract, ancl, therefore, it cannot be done. It Is for parliament to say that we want these additional terms, and if these additional terms are exacted, there is every reason to believe they will be conceded. If they are not accepted by the Grand Trunk Company, it will be evidence of this dangerous partnership between the two companies.
I do not like this silent partnership business at all ; but if we are to have a sleeping partner, let us have him out into the open and make a contract with him that he will have to stand by.

It is conceded that what is known as the western division of thi. railway will be the first part to be undertaken, or if not the first part to be undertaken, it will be the first part that will be constructed by the company building it. That is plain, owing to the fact that the requirements of the road will demand that that part shall be first constructed, and in the next place, that the construction of what is known as the prairie section of the railway will facilitate the building and the construction of the road through the mountains much faster than the eastern part. I think throughout the discussion it has been assumed that the road from Winnipeg eastward will not be constructed and in operation for some seven or eight years. In the meantime, therefore, it is idle to suppose that the Grand Trunk Pacific will have on their hands a large section of road extending from Edmonton to Winnipeg doing nothing. Therefore, it will be the duty of the Grand Trunk Pacific to look after an outlet for their grain. That outlet, I assume, must be secured by one of three courses : First, to make terms with the Canadian Pacific Railway for the transit of grain from Winnipeg to the head of Lake Superior ; second, to build a line from Winnipeg southward to the border and then make connection with the Northern Pacific to Duluth ; or there is a third course open, and that is to make arrangements with Mackenzie & Mann by which they would have the user of the Canadian Northern also to a point on the north end of Lake Superior, at Port Arthur.
A glance at the map will show any hon. gentleman the fact that there cannot be a distance of over 75 miles between the Canadian Northern Railway and the Northern Pacific running to Duluth. It is fair to assume that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, pouring its grain into Winnipeg and looking for an avenue outward to the east, will make one of these three arrangements instead pf running away north when the road is practically completed eastward and then running their branch south of it down by way of Lake Nepigon or to Port Arthur or Fort William. So it is fair to assume that for the first seven or eight years when the company are pouring their grain into Winnipeg which is a distributing point, the route Mr. LENNOX.
eastward is going to be by some of the routes which I have specified. Certainly, it is not going to be by a new railway built by themselves to the head of Lake Superior but rather by some easier arrangement that perhaps can be entered into. I think as far as clauses 42 and 43 are concerned, if the hon. Minister of Justice would give a frank answer, he would say that they are utterly useless for the purpose of compelling the Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry out this agreement, because the clauses themselves must of necessity be carried out by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. What do the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company agree to do ? They say that any freight not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports. To give an illustration, we know that in the city of Toronto there are the great works of the Massey-Harris people who m'ake large shipments of agricultural implements to the Northwest Territories. Is any man insane enough to believe that when this road is constructed the Massey-Harris Company would make an arrangememt with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to have their goods shipped to North Bay, and from North Bay hundreds of miles north to meet its line of railway ? In view of the fact that they would have communications opened with the head of Lake Superior, whether at Duluth or by arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Mackenzie & Mann system, these goods would be shipped from Colling-wood, Midland or Meaford, which are all points on the Grand Trunk Railway system proper, and they would be shipped to the head of Lake Superior and on to Winnipeg, which, as my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) suggests, is 300 miles shorter. Let any hon. gentleman go to Owen Sound and what will he find ? The Canadian Pacific Railway have probably 300 or 400 men employed during the season of navigation there handling package freight and other goods because the Canadian Pacific Railway prefer to send this freight to Owen Sound, to tranship it to their boats, take it to the head of Lake Superior and then place it on cars. An exactly similar course would be followed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company instead of carrying a large quantity of freight by a circuitous route. As far as the guarantee by the Grand Trunk Railway Company proper and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as to the routing of freight goes, it amounts to very little. Now, in clause 43 the government anticipated this very matter because the government say that they will bind this company to carry all freight to a Canadian port as cheaply as they would to an American port, or, to Portland. maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems remarkable, that, when we have a meteorological service extending throughout the Dominion of Canada with important points of information throughout the territories, up to the present time there has been an absolute and utter misapprehension in the minds of the general public in Canada and in the old country as well, as to the extent and results of this storm. It seems to me desirable that the attention of the government should be drawn to that fact. Had the storm been treated in an ordinary way by the purveyors of news throughout the country it would mot have been necessary to draw public attention to these facts. But when the opportunity has been taken, for what reason I am unable to say, to spread reports which are damaging and which are very largely incorrect it is a time when we might expect that our meterological service would put the matter right before the country, would in fact have kept the matter right and not have allowed it to have gone wrong. I wish to speak of the extent of the storm and it is on that point that I think the meterological department was very greatly in fault in not having given information as to the limits to which the storm extended. My information is that on the Saturday of the storm, the 13th instant, at Edmonton, there was no storm whatever. There was no knowledge of any storm at that time. The papers report a golf tournament taking place on that day, a very successful one in fact, so that it is evident there could have been no serious break in the weather on that particular day. It seems surprising that there should have been a report generally circulated throughout Canada and extended to the old country that this storm was universal and destructive throughout the territories. It has been surprising to me in view of the statements which have appeared even in the eastern press that the facts should not have been made known. I do not know where our eastern papers get their news service from the territories, but it seems certainly as if they have been very short of information, when they have allowed for over a week such misapprehensions, such misstatements and such damaging misstatements to be circulated generally throughout the country and throughout the world to go. so far as I have seen, uncontradicted. It Is not desirable to bring such matters up in parliament but under all- the circumstances it seems to be the only remedy for a very remarkable condition of affairs.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: I do not agree at all with my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that the first false reports which were put in circulation have not been contradicted. Everybody knows that the first report of this remarkable severe storm having done damage in the North-west is an absolute falsehood. Everybody who has read the newspapers knows by this time that the storm has been very limited in its area and not at all severe. Unfortunately, when an item appears in a newspaper, it is usually copied by all others, whether it is right or wrong. I do not know that there is any remedy for that;, they have no opportunity of verifying it. If it is right, well and good; if it is wrong, serious damage may be done. But I think everybody knows by this time that, happily for us, the storm was not of the character reported, and did no serious damage.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext:
The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) has very correctly described the route pursued by the storm. Although I have not seen any report from the Canadian meteorological service, the American service has traced the route of the storm as northeasterly, crossing the south-western corner of Manitoba, and passing on to James bay and the coast of Labrador. There is nothing at all surprising in the supposition that there has been a storm generally over north-western Canada. We find by the European newspapers that four weeks ago a heavy snow-storm broke over Saxony and certain parts of Austria ; and there has been scarcely a month in the present year when frosts have not occurred in southern New York and Pennsylvania. But what I rise to call attention to is that a certain officer of the meteorological department in Toronto was in the North-west in the vicinity of Edmonton about this time last year, when a hail-storm occurred that did some damage in a strip about five miles in area near Westaskiwin ; and that on his return home he wrote a description of the country in which he stated that in the district north of Wetaskiwin and Red Deer, though it might be possible to grow' oats, it would be utterly impossible to grow wheat ; although only three weeks before that gentleman had visited the locality, as any one familiar with the country knows, wheat had been cut in immense quantities, and had been marketed for from 100 to 150 miles north of the very spot where this gentleman stated that it would be utterly impossible for wheat to grow. I drew the attention of the government at the time to the report of this officer. I think that before these officers turn out immigration literature for the benefit of Texas. Louisiana and other parts of the south-western states, to the development of which our American friends are rightly directing their

attention, and to prevent settlers coming to Canada, the government should see that they know whereof they speak. This is not the first time that these erroneous reports have been sent to the old country. Had not Lord Strathcona happened to he in Canada the other day, I presume there would have been no official correction of this false report which some fellow in a back office in the city of Toronto telegraphed to the London ' Morning Post' and which was then telegraphed throughout the United Kingdom. Such a telegram stating that not 10 per cent of the entire crop of the Canadian North-west would be harvested, would have had a magical effect upon immigration to Canada; and the fact that Lord Strathcona took occasion to obtain reports from the North-west and forward them to the old country tended to remove the false impression. But that action was quite incidental, and if it had not been taken, it is hard to estimate the amount of damage that would have been done to Canada.

speechtext: F, CLARKE (West Toronto). I think the hon. member for West Assiniboia has done the country a good service in drawing attention to the exaggerated reports published in the old country as to the damage done by the snow-storm in the North-west. It is not pretended, I suppose, that Mr. Stupart was responsible for the reports which came to him from the different meteorological stations in Manitoba and the North-west. I should think that the local observers would have something to do with the despatch of the reports and the statements made with regard to the direction of the storm.

speechtext: Weather reports are sent in twice a day to the head office from every point in Manitoba and the territories.

maintopic: THE RECENT SNOWSTORMS IN THE NORTH-WEST.
speechtext: X quite understand that, and I presume that the reports which are compiled in the head office at Toronto and distributed, are based on the local reports received from the sections affected. I do not rise, however, to prolong the discussion, but respectfully to suggest to the government that if they desire to ascertain who are at fault, the reports sent to the head office at Toronto from the western stations should be carefully examined ; and if it is found that they are exaggerated, those responsible for sending them should be reprimanded ; because certainly great damage might have been done to western Canada by the transmission of these exaggerated reports across the Atlantic. I am satisfied, as I am sure every other hon. member must be, that the executive officers of the Meteorological Department at Toronto would not willingly or knowingly send exaggerated reports broadcast, but" that they were justified in making up their bulletins from the reports received from their representatives in the west.

speechtext: I would like to explain what I think is a misapprehension on the part of the members who have spoken as to the question at issue. It is not charged that the office in Toronto circulated reports that were not justified by the information received. What is charged is, that it did not circulate reports as to good weather according to information which it must have received.
