speechtext: That surely ought to be a matter of departmental investigation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one fact which I wish for a moment to refer to, and which may have some bearing on this matter ; that is, that in the states of Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota, this dip in the temperature did more damage than it did in the Canadian North-west. The weather was quite as severe in those states as in the region affected in the Canadian North-west. Although no snow fell there was frost enough to injure the corn crop and to do much more serious damage than any that was inflicted on our own country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment reads :
That section 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subsections :[DOT]-
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, or in the said agreement contained, ' His Majesty the King, acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of the covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty, the King, acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company shall covenant and agree as follows :-
(a.) That the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the balance required for the complete construction of the western division of the said agreement as provided in clause 34 of the said agreement.

The first two paragraphs of this amendment are merely intended, as I understand, to give effect to the agreement as it has been at all times understood and interpreted by the government. We have never at any time expected, nor was it even in contemplation, between the parties to the agreement, that the government should endorse or become liable for the first issue of bonds until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada had undertaken to guarantee the second issue. Therefore, with regard to the first and second paragraphs, we are prepared to accept this amendment, as it is in accord with the intentions of the parties. With regard to the third section, it is impossible for us to accept the amendment.

I desire to say a word with regard to clause (a). If the minister will turn to page 11623 of the unrevised ' Hansard,' he will see there the resolution as I gave notice of it. I would suggest that possibly the wording of clause (a), which my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is disposed to accept might be improved if it were made to read :
That ithe Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall guarantee thie 'bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for such an amount as shall produce and provide a sum of money equal to the balance required for the complete construction of the western division as provided in clause 34 of the said agreement.
Is my hon. friend (Mi-. Borden, Halifax) adopting the terms of the contract ?

No, I am not. The hon. gentleman will see exactly what the difference is between what I first proposed and the amendment which I now suggest. The amendment I now suggest

takes into consideration the possibility of the bond* guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company selling below par ; and, therefore, instead of saying that they should guarantee the bonds for the balance, I say that they shall guarantee the bonds to an amount sufficient to produce a sum of money equal to the balance required to complete construction of the western division.
As I understand, subclause (a), as my hon, friend first introduced it, adopts the words of section 34 of the contract ?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman now wishes to depart from that and make an amendment which would have the effect of altering to some extent the terms of the agreement ?

Of course, it alters the terms of the agreement in any case, even as at first proposed, because it provides that the Grand Trunk shall enter into a contract to do a particular thing. To that extent, and to that extent only, does it alter the terms of the agreement in clause 34. It provides that the bonds to be guaranteed shall be of sufficient amount to provide a sum of money equal to the balance required for the construction of the western division. That is all.

The contract provides that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall guarantee bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the balance required for the construction of the western division. That would be secured, I think, under the amendment the hon. gentleman first proposed. But, at first sight, I would not be disposed to depart from the terms of the agreement.

I should think that the words used in the amendment to the amendment really express what the government intended. I could hardly imagine that the government was simply asking the Grand Trunk Company to guarantee a sum of money equal to the balance that was required, without considering the probability of the bonds not producing the money. The government must surely have considered what position the country would be landed in, if after it had guaranteed three-quarters of the cost, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company had given their guarantee for the remaining quarter, the proceeds of the bonds so guaranteed should uot be sufficient to complete the railway. The result would be, as the Minister of Justice must see, that the work would come to a standstill unless the government or somebody else provided more money. In drawing the agreement, the government could never have intended that. It must have been the intention of the government that, after they had guaranteed bonds equal in amount to three-quarters of the cost, the Grand Trunk Railway Company Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
should assist the Grand Trunk Pacific to provide all the money required to complete the road. That, I take it, is, beyond question, what the government intended ; and if they did not clearly express that in the agreement, then, by this clause, we should express what they really did intend. I submit to the hon. minister that this requires very careful consideration.

The clear intention of the parties to the agreement- and we say that that intention is abundantly manifest in every line of the contract-is that the company should first get from the government the guarantee of bonds to the amount of 75 per cent of the cost of construction, and whatever is required over and above that must be guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That is expressed in terms :
Inasmuch as the bonds to be guaranteed by the government only make provision for a part of the cost of construction of the western division. the company hereby agrees that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall guarantee bonds of the company for itbe balance required for the constructing of the said western division.
The intention of the parties is clear,- all that is required for the construction of the western division, above the proportion guaranteed by the government, is to be provided under bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk. I do not see how it is improved by this proposed amendment.

It was probably the intention of the parties to provide as the hon. minister lias said ; but it is very important for us to consider whether the agreement as drawn expresses that. Let me put the case to the hon. minister. Suppose the cost of the western division to be one hundred millions. The government would not be called upon to guarantee more than seventy-five millions.
That would be the outside possible limit.

Now, then, the Grand Trunk will be called upon to guarantee bonds to provide the remaining $25,000,000. The hon. gentleman says they must guarantee bonds that will produce $25,000,000. Let us seo what the wording is :
The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall! guarantee bonds of the company for the balance required for the construction of the said western division, exclusive of the said $20,000,000 required for first equipment.
In the case I put, the balance required for the construction of the western division is $25,000,000 ; therefore, this language clearly says that the Grand Trunk in that case shall guarantee bonds for $25,000,000, although It might require bonds for $30,000,-to produce the $25,000,000 cash.
The language does not imply any such construction, in my opinion.

The hon. gentleman thinks so, but is the meaning plain ? Assume that $25,000,000 is required to complete the road, then the Grand Trunk shall guarantee the bonds of the company for the balance required for construction. ' Guarantee bonds for the balance,' that is, for the amount of the balance, not bonds which, when sold upon the market, will produce that balance. That is the point of the amendment here, and I think, with all due respect to the Minister of Justice, that it will be a serious thing if it is not expressed in the clearest possible language. You will probably find that the Grand Trunk will look upon it in a very different light. There can be no question I take it, that the second mortgage bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk will not sell at par. I do not care what rate of interest you may give, what reasonable rate of interest you put upon those bonds, 4 per cent, or any reasonable rate, I do not believe they will sell at par upon the market. Very well, then it is perfectly clear that whatever may be the actual balance in money required to complete the road, you will have to issue more bonds to realize that balance. Does the Minister of Justice say the contract is clearly expressed in this respect ?
I think so.

Will the hon. gentleman say it is not open to argument?
TheJ MINISTER OF JUSTICE. I would not say that, because ray hon. friend does argue it, but if he had not argued it I would have said it. I would not like to say that after my hon. friend has expressed his opinion.

I am obliged to the hon. gentleman for the compliment. But I repeat again, the words do not clearly convey the meaning expressed in the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition, that the Grand Trunk shall guarantee bonds that will produce the balance required. Supposing I asked the hon. gentleman to endorse my note for $1,000. I doubt if the hon. gentleman would do it. But supposing I made that request to the hon. gentleman, and then I said, Oh, I can't get that note cashed at par. I want you to endorse it for $1,100-would the hon. gentleman think that the same thing ? To my mind, this language expresses the very opposite of what the hon. gentleman says. You are to ascertain your balance, and they are to guarantee bonds for the balance, not bonds that will produce that balance. The hon. gentleman says it is intended that they guarantee bonds that will produce the balance. We ask that that shall be expressed in so many words, so that there will be no doubt.

I accept the amendment suggested by the leader of
the opposition, because I am convinced that his amendment only carries out the construction both parties put upon the contract.

Of course, the only difficulty that arises is that upon a somewhat careful examination of the language of clause 34, it was the opinion of some gentlemen on this side of the House, that there might be at least a question with regard to the point my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has raised. My hon. friend from Hamilton says that when you look at the expression ' the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall guarantee bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the balance required,' you are to understand that as being the amount of the balance required. The Minister of Justice would seem to dissent from that view, but I d<o not know exactly upon what ground, for the balance required means certainly the amount of the balance required. If it does not mean that, what does it mean ? The Minister of Finance suggests it does not say that, then what other meaning can you attach to it ? The Grand Trunk Company is to guarantee bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for some amount. The question is whether that amount as expressed in subclause (a) is such an amount as will realize the balance required ; or whether it is simply the amount of -the balance required. I am inclined to think there is a great deal of force in the argument of my hon. friend from Hamilton, that when you use the expression ' for the balance required,' that means for the amount of the balance required, but it does not mean a sum of money which will realize, when the bonds are sold in the market, the balance required, for completing the construction of the western division. The question between us is one of the construction of words. One would suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if this construction were attacked, would be entitled to say, These words are to be construed in no strained sense against us ; but when you provide by this clause that we are to guarantee bonds for the balance required, it means exactly what it says, the amount of the balance required, the amount which is represented by the balance required ; but it does not mean an amount of bonds which, when sold in the market, will realize the balance required. That is exactly the point my hon. friend from Hamilton makes.

It strikes me the expression ' balance required ' means the balance required. I remember at one time when the question of the resumption of specie payment was raised in the United States, Horace Greeley said, ' The right way to resume is to resume.' I think the balance required is the balance required, and I do not think we can use any other words

to express it more clearly. What the hon. gentleman aims at and what we aim at is precisely the same thing. We are fully advised that that is already provided in the Act. Take the suggestion of the hon. member for Hamilton that this road is to cost $100,000,000, of which the government will guarantee three-fourths, and they will require to raise $25,000,000 more. Now, is it reasonable to believe that if the Grand Trunk guaranteed bonds to the amount of $24,000,000 and discovered that there was another million needed, they would absolutely sacrifice their $24,000,000 for the sake of that forced interpretation of the contract? The Grand Trunk, in its own interest, for the sake of the protection of their road, would be obliged to see that the bonds produced the balance required to finish the work, otherwise this $24,000,000 would be absolutely wasted. The Grand Trunk Company could not afford to do that, and that is perhaps one of the strongest arguments. Of course, we say that they could not do it lawfully. But, for their own protection, they could not afford to put any difference between the nominal value of the bonds and their selling price. But, over and above that, we claim they are obliged to do it legally.

The Minister of Finance, I think, fails to realize the point. That is probably owing to his lack of legal training. The point is not a question of expediency, it is a question of construction and a question of law, a question of what the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be compelled, beyond doubt, to do.
The hon. Minister of Justice said this morning at the opening of this matter that he was prepared to accept clause (a) as suggested by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) the other day because it carried out the intention of the government at the time it entered into this contract. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition now thinks upon further consideration that the intention of the government might be made more clear by the amendment as he proposes it this morning and there can be no doubt, I think, that the wording of the amendment as proposed this morning is more specific and satisfactory than the one which was suggested the other day. Now, it is a question of construction as to wfliether the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be bound to merely guarantee the bonds for nominal amount of the balance or for the actual amount required. I take it-and I say this with all due deference to the hon. Minister of Justice-that clause 34 of the contract is not clear as establishing the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be bound to do more than guarantee the bonds for the nominal amount required to complete the railway ; in other words, that after the government have provided for 75 per cent of the total cost and Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
have ascertained what the total cost is under the contract, the position of the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be this : Bonds may be issued for what appears to be the nominal balance, the difference between the amount guaranteed by the government and the actual amount that the railway has cost. The Grand Trunk Railway Company are bound to guarantee these bonds for their face value and they are not bound to guarantee any more. I say this, of course, with a feeling of hesitation by reason of the fact that the hon. Minister of Justice has expressed a different opinion, but notwithstanding the fact that such an eminent authority has expressed a different opinion I feel so convinced that I would urge upon the hon. Minister of Justice to further consider the question. The clause says :
' Shall guarantee bonds of the company for the balance.' Assuming that the balance is $25,000,000. the Grand Trunk Railway Company might with great reason and force say : Present your bonds for $25,000,000 and we will guarantee those bonds. We have nothing whatever to do with the question of how much the bonds will produce. We have agreed to guarantee the bonds for a specific amount, wq guarantee the bonds for that specific amount and whether they shall produce a sufficient amount or not does not concern us because it is not covered by the contract. They are exactly upon the same plane as the person who undertakes to endorse a promissory note for an individual for, say, $25,000. He endorses the note but after he has endorsed the note he has fulfilled his contract. If the note does not produce the amount required by the person who has received the accommodation, the man who has endorsed is not responsible. That is the position of the Grand Trunk Railway Company under this contract. The hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) says that this is a matter of saving themselves and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be compelled to come to the rescue. That is not the point. The point is to make this contract clear to all Intents and purposes and it is not as clear as it should be under clause 34. The hon. Minister of Justice practically admits that. He says :	We are perfectly willing to
adopt the clause as suggested the other day, clause (a), by the hon. leader of the opposition. If the hon. Minister of Justice is prepared to adopt clause (a), as suggested the other day. I submit that there is every reason for accepting the clause which is moved this morning because it makes it clear beyond doubt that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are responsible for whatever balance there may be required for the construction of the railway and that they should guarantee the bonds not to the extent of their nominal value, but to the) extent of an amount sufficient to cover the
balance of the cost of the construction of the road. I understand that we are all

at all possible, carry the freight via Portland, or some American port. I am afraid there is not going to be any driving or forcing of grain by a Canadian route. These two clauses appear to me to be practiealiv worthless and might as well be dropped out of the Bill as well as some of those other absurd clauses as to the purchasing of goods in Canada and some others which have been discussed here. But, since the government are endeavouring to gain support for this scheme throughout the whole of Canada by the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are behind this enterprise let the ' Grand Trunk Railway Company be bound by it as far as possible. Take, for instance, a statement made by Mr. Hays upon one of the first days that this Bill was considered at the meeting of the Railway Committee. What did he say ? When asked whether this road would progress at the rate that had been suggested, he said :	With the immense powers we
have, with the great energy of the Grand Trunk Railway Company there should be a realization of our wishes and this road should be completed within a very few years. Throughout tire discussion not only in the Railway Committee, but in the House the statement has been made that the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were one and the same concern. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are going to get all the benefit and the prestige of the reputation of the old Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is something enormous in the eyes of the Canadian people, in order that this contract which is being entered into may be fully carried out, a provision such as that proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition should be inserted.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to what the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) have said. The hon. Minister of Finance has declared that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company are one and the same corporation after all. I do not wish to be misunderstood when I make use of that by saying that they are one corporation. They are separate corporations, but after all they have a common interest. The hon. Minister of Justice stated that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would in the nature of things be called upon to carry out in detail all that was contended for by the hon. leader of the opposition in his amendment. I do not know whether I accurately understood the hon. Minister of Justice in that statement. Whatever may be said about a violation of the letter of contract the hon. Minister of Justice will concede that the essence of the contract is not changed if the amendment o|f the hon1. leader of the opposition is adopted. If the essence of contract is not changed then no 372
injustice is done to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Why should there be any objection on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to amend any of the weak points in the company's contract with the country ? This is all one contract. After all, as the hon. Minister of Finance has said, we are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and with the Grand Trunk Railway Company as one and the samje company. True they are different corporations, but they are both in essence the same. If that be true why should the Grand Trunk Railway Company hesitate a single moment, or why should it be contended that there would be any violation of the contract in substance or in essence ? Let me repeat again what the hon. Minister of Finance says that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand1 Trunk Pacific Railway Companies are the same. Why should there be the slightest hesitation to enter into an agreement to carry out every portion of the contract being entered into with the Grand Truhk Pacific Railway Company, which is all under the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself ?	,
That is the way it strikes an ordinary layman like myself, and I am sure that is the way in which it will strike the public. If they were separate corporations, and one were called- in as a mere endorser, I could quite understand that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would contend that they had not undertaken all the obligations of the other Company, but in this case they are merely becoming guarantors for another .part of their own concern, which is under a different name. I cannot see that there would be the slightest injustice done to the Grand Trunk Railway Company by this amendment, and I fail"to see why they do not assent to it. Although I am not a lawyer, I can understand the difference between the spirit and the letter of a contract, and in this case it is perfectly plain1 that what we ask is just and right in the interests of Canada. The Minister of Finance contends that no matter what kind of contract is made, whether it is good, bad or indifferent, it cannot be changed by this parliament. That means that we must swallow the contract holus-bolus. Surely we are here to advocate and to adopt such changes as are necessary in the interests of the country. I can understand a contract being so bad that parliament might reject it it altogether. I will not say that this contract is of such a character, but undoubtedly there are bad features in it, and what is parliament if it cannot remove these objectionable features ? It seems to me that the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition is not only" reasonable, but there is absolutely no defence whatever for opposing it.

I wish to answer the hon. gentleman at once. I



say distinctly that where a contract between the government and another party is submitted to parliament for approval, you cannot change one line of that contract. Parliament can reject such a contract, but parliament cannot make a contract with the other party
Cannot parliament refer it back to have it amended?
That is another question.
That is what I said.

It is not what the hon. gentleman said. He condemned me for saying that this contract cannot be altered, and I repeat what I said in that respect. This contract cannot be altered by anything the parliament of Canada may do, and unless there be a mutual agreement to change the contract, it cannot be changed. I want to state that without any qualification Whatever. As to how far the Grand Trunk Company are m this and of it, I say that the Grand Trunk Company is in this enterprise to a degree which we regard as of very great value. In tlife first place, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Justice at the initiation of this enterprise, the sum of 85,000,000 must be put up. We know that at the beginning the Grand Trunk Pacific will not have acquired the money to put up that five millions, and practically, although it is not an obligation of the Grand Trunk, we know as a matter of fact, that the Grand Trunk Company must finance the Grand Trunk Pacific at the beginning, and before the latter company is fully organized. The promoters of this scheme, and that means practically the Grand Trunk, must put up five million dollars
Have they promised ?

The Grand Trunk Pacific have promised, aud the promoters of that company must so finance as to l'aise that five million dollars, and practically they will have to rely on the Grand Trunk to do it for them. The next point made by lion, gentlemen opposite is that we require the Grand Trunk to take the whole of this common stock. The fatal error in the argument of these hon. gentlemen is in assuming that this is a great advantage to the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk Company would be delighted to have that clause stricken out, so that they might be allowed to take the stock up and float it in the money market as they please. That, I have no doubt, would be more gratifying to the promoters of this enterprise. We have put that limitation in. not to please the Grand Trunk Company, but as an additional guarantee to the people that that stock is not going to be placed on the market and floated at a fictitious value. I say, unhesitatingly, that it would be better to give it to the Grand Trunk, even without any other condition than it would be to have Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
it dealt out to be used by stock speculators on the market. It is not fair to say that we are giving it to the Grand Trunk Company, because every one knows that under the provisions of the Railway Act, the Grand Trunk Company can only get it for value. However, that has been discussed over and over again, and I need not refer to it further. My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) said that the Grand Trunk is going to be behind this scheme, but so far behind that you cannot see the connection.
I do not see how the hon. gentleman makes that out, if the Grand Trunk Company has to have connection with the other company to the extent of guaranteeing these bonds for one-quarter the cost of the western section. The leader of the opposition, by way of illustration, said : Suppose that road costs a hundred million dollars, the government will only guarantee three-quarters, or not exceeding 75 per cent of that. They have to come right up to the captain's office and settle by their own guarantee to the extent of one-quarter of the cost. What is the use, then, of gentlemen opposite saying that the Grand Trunk Company are going to have no obligation in this matter at all ? And, because the Grand Trunk agree to give certain valuable guarantees, my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) comes forward and says that they ought to do something more. Well, we think that is not reasonable.

The statement of the Minister of Finance as to the obligation the Grand Trunk has assumed in guaranteeing 25 per cent of the cost, is answered by the claim which the hon. gentleman himself made to the House, that the government by guaranteeing 75 per cent of that cost, was not assuming any obligation whatever. That was the argument of the Finance Minister, and that is how he sought to prove that the country would only assume obligations to the extent of 813,000,000
I never said anything of the kind.

The Minister of Finance Stated that the total obligation of the country would only be ?13,000,000, and he brought to his support the statement of an expert actuary who made it less than 816,000,000, but in order to be in accord with the statement of the Prime Minister he said that he would put the figure at 813,000,000. Now, in order to arrive at his thirteen million dollar calculation, it was necessary for the Minister of Finance to contend that the 75 per cent guarantee on the western section would not cost the country one dollar. Here then, we have an answer to his latest argument that the Grand Trunk Railway Company. in assuming to guarantee the remaining 25 per cent of the cost of construction, is assuming an important obligation. They

have a mortgage over all the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific to secure them for their guarantee, and they get that mortgage as compensation from the Grand Trunk Pacific for giving that guarantee. One of the things they get is this $25,000,000 of common stock ; and yet the hon. gentleman says-I do not know what he thinks ; I must take what he says, because that may be 'entirely different from what he thinks-he says that it is better that this common stock should go into the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and be held by them for fifty years than that it should go upon the market, and that whatever value is realized from it in the open market should go into the construction of tile road. It seems to me that that is ft very strange argument. I grant that it is far better for the Grand Trunk Company ; but certainly it cannot be for the benefit of the people who are to use this railway, and who are to be taxed in the matter of freight rates for the cost of this road. Now, the hon. Minister of Finance claimed that it was necessary for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to have tills line built north of Lake Superior in order that the western division should be of any advantage to them. Every person on the other side of the House who has spoken, from the premier down, has admitted that it will take at least seven years to complete the eastern division, while the western division, as far west as the mountains, at any rate that part of it which is necessary to tap the wheat-growing part of the country, will be built and completed inside of two years. So that there will be five years during which there will be no connection between the western division and the eastern division ; and during those five years what is to become of the product ? My hon. friend says it will be more like ten years. I have no doubt that would be>
nearer the mark ; but I am taking the argument advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite. Where will the traffic of the western division go during those five years ? It will go south, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce lias pointed out, and be carried over the American lines to the connections with the Grand Trunk Railway ; and to prevent that is one reason why we are presenting this amendment, which will obligate the Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry all their Canadian traffic over Canadian lines to Canadian ports. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be unable to carry it to the east. The hon. Minister of Finance said that we had the Grand Trunk Railway Company bound by obligations. What are they ? We oblige them to take $25,000,000 of stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is a strange obligation, it seems to me. We are obliging them to take the stock ; we are not. obliging them to pay one dollar for it. If the hon. minister had fallen in with the proposal of the opposition, and forced the Grand Trunk Railway Company 372J
to pay par value for that stock, there would be something in his argument. But they may get the whole $25,000,000 without paying one dollar cash for it, or in return for guaranteeing the bonds on the western division. Then, he says, there is the obligation to guarantee the bonds. That is certainly not a very heavy burden on the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if the hon. gentleman .is right in his contention that it will not cost this country one dollar to guarantee 75 per cent of the bonds on the western division. That seems to me to be a perfect answer to the hon. gentleman's contention. We have heard a good deal about this $5,000,000 security that is to be put up for the .carrying out of this contract. Let us see what value there is in that security. This $5,000,000 has to be paid up within thirty days of the ratification of the contract. The hon. Minister of Finance assumes at once, without any authority, so far as the written contract is concerned, that that is going to be put up by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We have heard that great financial magnates are connected with this scheme. If that is the case, the putting up of $5,000,000, which they are to get back again, should not be a very serious matter to them, and it would not be necessary to call upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company for that. However, the hon. minister assumes that that is to be put up by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. What they may have said to him verbally does not bind them, as the hon. gentleman knows full well. You find by reading the contract that the $5,000,000 is to be returned, and is to go into the cost of the equipment of the eastern division. What has become of your $5,000,000 then ? It has been absorbed, and you have simply the equipment of the eastern division as your whole security for cai-rying out that lease. And, mark you, you have not the whole of that. You have only a second mortgage on that equipment, because, to secure the bonds that have fifty years to run, there is a mortgage given against everything, including the equipment on the eastern division. I think that only applies to the bonds issued to the government. The mortgage that secures the Grand Trunk Railway Company does not cover the equipment of the eastern division. Let us see what we have this great security figured down to. Instead of $5,000,000 to be deposited in the treasury of this country, we have simply a second mortgage on the $5,000,000 worth of equipment on the eastern division. We have that road seven years before any interest is paid ; then there are three years more in which the company may pay interest if they earn it. Of course, it goes without saying, that they will not earn it ; that is, so far as reports are concerned. They will take the full limit of ten years. Nobody would expect anything else. That equipment then will be ten years old before

the lease begins to operate, so far as any rental is concerned. Then, before you could enforce the terms of the lease for non-payment of rental, one year at least must elapse. Of course, a government would not be so sharp as to insist on the payment of the rental in the first year. All sorts of excuses could be brought by the railway company to induce the government to defer the payment for at least another year. Then you would have twelve years within which the equipment of this eastern division would be in use before you could begin to enforce your remedy.
Now, what would be more easy for the railway company, if they wished to protect their own interests at the expense of the country-and we all know how these things are worked, we know that men when doing business with the government are not so scrupulously honest as when doing business between individuals and that perhaps the government is not quite so strenuous in enforcing its claims as the individual with whom it is doing business-than to put on the eastern division of that road all their worn out engines and cars from the western division, or even to put on it their worn out equipment from the old Grand Trunk Railway. Then you would have on that line a lot of old worn out equipment nominally worth $5,000,000 but actually not worth $1,000,000. On this you have not a first mortgage but a second mortgage and if you should put the property up for a sale you would have to sell it subject to the first mortgage and how much would it bring, a lot of old scrap that has been in use at least twelve years, some of it perhaps for twenty years. This would be practically worthless so that the great security of which we have heard so much from hon. gentlemen opposite would have faded away. In making a contract you must look at the worst possible phase of it. It may be that the gentlemen who are now promoting this railway will carry out any verbal assurance they may give to the government, but fifty years from now they will have no connection with this company and in making a contract, especially for so long a time, you should provide for every possible contingency. It appears to me that the objections I have pointed out with respect to the security under this contract are so obvious that they cannot escape the view of any person who considers its terms.

It strikes me that the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has indulged in at least one or two fallacies in his discussion of this question. He makes a comparison between the character of the securities held by the Grand Trunk Railway and by the government on the western division and says that one is on a parity with the other, that if the government has a guarantee or security it is of a character that will not likely ever have to be paid, and that the security of the Grand Trunk Mr. FOWLER.
Railway Company is as good as that of the government. I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman. The government guarantees the bonds of the company to an amount equivalent to three-quarters of the cost of the road. It takes as security for that guarantee the road itself, its own investment in the road, the company's investment of twenty-five per cent more, and the company's investment for rolling stock on the road amounting to $15,000,000. Or if the road cost $100,000,000 the government takes as security $25,000,000 of investment of the company in the road and $15,000,000 of rolling stock, a total of $40,000,000 supplied by the company and in addition its own $75,000,000, making in all $115,000,000 on which the government holds a first mortgage as security for its advance of $75,000,000. As the company takes the position of a second mortgage in this matter it is in a position entirely different from that of the government.
For what does the government hold that security ?

The government guarantees three-quarters of the cost of the road and holds as security the amount of that investment besides an additional Investment, one-fourth as large, and the rolling stock of the company. The government's security is ample; the company's security is a second mortgage security and if the property is not worth its cost the loss will fall first upon the company that holds the second mortgage and ultimately, if there is a deficiency, upon the government. But there is no possibility that any such deficiency will ever exist. My hon. friend has given a presentation of the case calculated to mislead public opinion and to create an impression on the country which is the reverse of the fact, to create an impression that the government have been careless and slip-shod in their method of making this contract.. This is not the case; the government, so far ns the western section is concerned, has taken ample security, is in a strong position and cannot stand to lose.
Then my hon. friend goes on to tell us that the western division will be built in two years and the eastern division cannot be built in less than seven years. A line, 1,450 miles in length, from Quebec to Winnipeg is to require seven years to construct.

Will my hon. friend permit me to correct him, I said that that portion towards the mountains, from Winnipeg to the mountains would be built in two years. That is the part of it that touches the grain district.

The section from Winnipeg to the Rockies will extend a distance of about 1,350 miles, lacking about one hundred miles of the length of the line from Winnipeg to Quebec and to construct this 1,350 miles my hon. friend says will take two years, while the other division, 100 miles

longer, will take seven years. These statements are preposterous, simply preposterous. The hon. gentleman concedes that the eastern section is essential to the success of the western section, it will be an outlet for the western section and for other roads at Winnipeg. What is to hinder as rapid construction of the eastern section as of the western section ? It passes through a country where material for ties, piles, and to a certain extent for bridges, cam be obtained, whereas with the western section all the supplies will have to be transported long distances. In my opinion the eastern section can be constructed more rapidly than the western.
Oh, oh.

It is my opinion that it can. These gentlemen have been talking of this country north of the height of land as a bog, as a great stretch of peat, as a country perfectly valueless, with no resources at all. Sir, it can .be proved to be a country which can furnish homes for millions of people, a country of great agricultural resources and adapted for business in other lines. The railway through this can be built almost simultaneously with the western section.
My hon. friend goes on to talk of the putting of worn-out engines and rolling stock upon this eastern section. A company operating a road of the character that this road will be, with slight grades, will in its own interest, to secure profitable operation, put on it an equipment sufficient and efficient to do the work cheaply and thoroughly. It will have no object in doing anything else. Then, he talks about the deposit of $5,000,000 as no security at all, and says it is not put up by the Grand Trunk, and so on. What does it matter who puts it up ? If the $5,000,000 is put as security for the western construction, the security is forthcoming. And he tells us that that can be withdrawn as the work progresses. It can be withdrawn only at a time when its withdrawal will secure the completion of the work.
What work ?

The western section. When the western section is completed, the purpose for -which the deposit is made ceases. It is made as security for the western section, and it is provided that the government may allow that $5,000,000 to be used to secure completion, that the company will be obliged absolutely to complete the road before it can use the money; but if it is within $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 of completion, it can avail itself of the deposit. And the hon. gentleman, in the course of his remarks, asserts that the interest for the full period of ten years will unquestionably be paid by the government. Suppose it is, the contract provides for that emergency. It provides that the government shall pay the interest for seven years, and then, if the company is unable to pay for three
years, the government adds that interest to the capital account and the company must pay interest on that whole account for the remainder of the fifty years. What difference does it make whether the company pays the interest for the last three years or whether it is added to the capital account and the company pays interest upon it ? I do not hold with the hon. gentleman that the company will be unable to pay interest at the expiration of the seven years. I believe that the government has allowed the company to refrain from paying interest for a longer period than was necessary. I believed that at the outset. I believed that it was unnecessary to give the company more than five years, for in five years from the completion of the road, the company will be in a position to pay interest and all charges. I believe that still. I do not apprehend that there is the slightest probability of the company being in straits at the end of seven years. I believe, on the contrary, that by that time this road will have developed this business and will be one of the best railway properties in America. It will be the great outlet of the west. It will be able to lay down in Quebec the products of the wheat fields of the west cheaper than any other route, whether all-rail or rail and water. The surveys have progressed so far that we know to-day practically what the line will be. The Trans-Canada Company surveyed several hundred miles from the eastern extremity westward. The Grand Trunk Pacific has surveyed from Winnipeg to a point north-east of Lake Nepigon. The Grand Trunk Pacific have secured four-tenths per cent grades. The Trans-Canada has secured six-tenths per cent grades, but their chief engineer said that had it been an object to get four-tenths per cent grades, they could have got them ; they were seeking six-tenths which was the best they had on the Great Northern. We know to-day that more than three-fifths of this road has been surveyed and on that portion four-tenths per cent grades can be secured. And we know that the character of the country between the points to which the surveys have reached are such that we can count at least as good a line as in any portion of the country that has been surveyed. If this is true that road will do the business of the North-west. You do not need to figure as to whether that road can pay interest or whether it will be equipped with wheezy old broken-down engines. It will be carrying trains with two thousand tons of freight.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) laughs. Well, he laughs best who laughs last. By the time this road is completed, we shall see. Here we have these pessimistic speculations, these misrepresentations-whether made for a purpose or not, I 'do not know-these misrepresentations and pessimistic forecasts with regard to a

scheme which is tQ be a nation builder for Canada, an undertaking which will carry itself, a road which will be worth double its cost by the time the government conies into its possession, at the end of fifty years. And we are haggling over this scheme. I am surprised. We are making representations not at all consistent with common sense or business principles. It would be better to settle down to business, to get the road started to satisfy ourselves that the government's security is ample-as it is- and to let the scheme go through ; instead of staying here until December talking about things and advancing opinions of the character talked about and advanced in this House.

If any other lion, geutle-man on the other side of the House had made the reckless statements which the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has made, I would have been surprised. But, knowing the reputation of that lion, gentleman along that line, knowing the sort of statements he makes to-day and contradicts to-morrow, I am not surprised at what he has said. He betrays an absolute ignorance of the terms of the contract.
Oh, oh.

I repeat it-an absolute ignorance of the terms of the contract. He has said that this $5,000,000 whicii is supposed to be put up, is security for the construction of the eastern division. Those are the very words the hon. gentleman used, and he used them more than once. And he said that as soon as the eastern division is completed this money is paid over. If the hon. gentleman had read the contract, he would have known that the $5,000,000 is security that the eastern division shall be equipped. Why should $5,000,000 be put up as security for the construction of the eastern division, when the government is to construct that portion of the line ? Now, if this is a sample of the way in which the hon. gentleman will discuss the matter throughout the country, how much reliance can be placed on his statements with regard to the surveys he has talked about ? He says these surveyors have reported that they have found a line on which a road can be built that will haul trains of 2,000 tons weight-such trains, I suppose, as he spoke of in his big speech on this subject, when he said that the train crews objected to having trains more than a mile long. Where does the hon. gentleman get his information? Where are the reports of these surveyors that he talks so glibly about ? If the hon. gentleman were not a member of parliament, I might make an observation or two with regard to such statements which might not be considered complimentary by the hon. gentleman. But, Mr. Chairman, knowing what a stickler you are for the rules of debate, I am obliged to restrain myself. It is not out of order for me to say, bow-Mr. CHARLTON.
ever, that the hon. gentleman's statements are about on a par with the statement of the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the government had mountains of information with regard to that country, and when they laid it before this House it looked not at all like a mountain, but more like a hole in the ground. The hon. gentleman (Ml-. Charlton) is a little off with respect to his distances. He does not agree with himself. I suppose that when he made his first speech on this subject, he had been instructed. He told us that this prairie section was 1,200 miles long. Today he has it about 1.350 miles long. The eastern section, according to the Minister of Finance, is 1,875, miles long.
From Moncton.

So, instead of there being a difference of 100 miles, as the hon. gentleman- said a while ago, there is a difference of about GOO miles, according to the statements of himself and the Minister of Finance. Well, that is about as near as the hon. gentleman can get to the fact. If the fact is GOO miles, he says 100 miles, and so be only gets within 500 miles of the fact. That shows just about the amount of truth in the statements of the hon. gentleman.
Now, he accuses us of haggling. Let everything go, he says. Why discuss this contract ? Why talk about it ? The 14 or 15 gentlemen who represent the cabinet-I do not know how many there are now, there have been so many resignations lately-but supposing there are 14 or 15 gentlemen, he says they have made a certain contract, and the 213 members of this House should let it go, because the cabinet represents, I suppose, the united wisdom of all the members of this House. Now, that does seem to me a very strange position for a business man to take, and I suppose we may consider him a business man-that we should enter into a contract for 50 years, a contract involving such a large amount of money as this contract will involve, and yet we are not to discuss the terms of it; if we do, if we attempt to improve it in any way, why, we are simply haggling. This is a very strange position surely for a member of this House, having upon him the responsibility of a representative of the people, it is a very peculiar position for the hon. gentleman to take. What is the matter ? Does he see looming up in the distance another meeting of the International Conference, and so he wants to let everything go in regard to this road. Is that the reason why the hon. gentleman has changed his view from the 23rd of May last when he opposed this whole scheme, when he denounced this scheme, denounced it publicly ? There must be some reason for it. I do not like to impute sinister motives to hon. gentlemen in this House, but when we see such a sudden bolt, such a quick turn by an hon. gentleman, a business man, too
And a Christian.

That goes without saying, all the members of this House are Christians, of course-when we see a man like this, who has a certain reputation as a business man, and who surely would not make a statement off-hand about a measure so important as a transcontinental railway project, we must assume therefore that the statement of the 23rd of May must have been a well-considered statement, he surely must have felt his responsibility as a member of parliament, his responsibility as a public man, as a member of the party, when he was opposing this thing, for he knew that, in making that statement, he was flying in the face of the premier of this country, the leader of his party, in fact in the face of his whole party-therefore, I assume that the statement which the hon. gentleman made on the 23rd of May was a careful and well-considiered statement, after having weighed the pros and cons of the whole subject. He then delivered himself of that statement on the 23rd of May, in which he denounced in round terms this whole project, lock, stock and barrel. The hon. gentleman certainly was not talking then along the line of letting everything go, and accusing us of haggling because we criticise the terms of this contract. Not at all. What then has wrought so sudden a conversion in the hon. gentleman's mind? Surely it is not the argument brought forward by the premier respecting the necessity of this road, surely he was not frightened by the ghost of the withdrawal of the bonding privilege, that cheap scarecrow. What is it ? Has he become so converted to Cana-dianism, has he at last become so patriotic a Canadian that the idea of one pound of Canadian freight being carried over a foot of American soil is so revolting to the hon. gentleman that he is willing to retract his statement of the 23rd of May ? How can we account for it ? There is only one of these three things that will account for it ; I believe he was converted, I believe he was frightened by that bogey of the abrogation of the bonding privilege; or else his patriotic soul revolted at the idea of Canadian freight being carried over American soil by American lines; or else he saw looming up in the not distant future another meeting of the International Conference, and he did not want to be left out of it. Now, the hon. gentleman can take either one of these alternatives that he sees fit. But I do say that it looks very strange for an hon. gentleman like this to say that we are haggling be^ cause we, feeling the responsibility upon us as members of parliament, seek to perfect the scheme as much as possible, and to safeguard the best interests of the people of this country.
Now, the hon. gentleman makes another assertion; ne says that we on this side have been abusing this country, that we have
been speaking of it as a country absolutely worthless. I hurl that assertion back into the teeth of the hon. gentleman. I say no man on this side has spoken in disparaging terms of any portion of this Canada of ours. We are not that sort of a party, that is not a characteristic of the Conservative party ever since that party was formed in this country. Our policy has always been the upbuilding of this country, the proper and due exploitation of the resources of this country; and therefore no man calling himself a Conservative would ever for a moment attempt to say anything derogatory of any portion of this country. We have said that this is not an attractive country, that it is not a country through which it would be easy to build a railway; we have said! that, from the very conformation of the country, it would not be easy to build such a line as is apparently intended by this Bill, that is, such a line as would be useful as a transcontinental road for the purpose of competing against American roads to the south. We say that the conformation of that country is such that it would be impossible to get proper grades to haul such trains as the member for North Norfolk has spoken about. It is all very well for that hon. gentleman, without a shadow of proof, without being able to adduce one statement of any responsible person, of any responsible surveyor, without being able to bring before this Committee one report from a surveyor of that district-it is all very well for him to get up and say thatti it is possible to build this road with four-tenth per cent grades, when he absolutely) knows no more about it than does any other hon. gentleman in this House, and far less; than some of them, notwithstanding the certificate which the Prime Minister has given him of being the greatest railway expert on this North American continent. Where did this hon. gentleman get his railway experience ? We know that he has been largely engaged in lumbering operations, but we never heard of that hon. gentleman as a railway builder, or a railway owner, or that he ever took a course of civil engineering, or has had any experience in that line. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) suggests that his railway experience has been acquired by building a track to carry the sawdust and edgings from his mill to the place where it was burned. I suppose that is the only railway building he knows anything about, except what he has learned by travelling over them on a pass like the rest of us. I fail to see any reason why the Prime Minister should call the member for North Norfolk a railway expert, except it might be becaue he knew so little about railways. I trust, Sir, that before the hon. member for North Norfolk again stands up and attempts to lecture the members on this side of the House, he will gather together some actual facts and talk upon them, instead of basing his state-

ments upon such distortions of facts as lie has done in the statement he has just made. It has been suggested that there is an alternative proposition the hon. gentleman lias in view, instead of attending again the International Conference, namely, that the hon. gentleman is attempting to qualify for the vacant portfolio of railways, and perhaps that is why the premier gave him this certificate of character as a railway expert. We know that the hon. gentleman has been anxious for many years past to become a member of this cabinet. We know that the hon. gentleman got so rusty about the last election that he published a manifesto in which he declared his independence and that the Conservative party in his part of the country were willing, although I do not know why they should have been, to accept his statement and allowed him his election by acclamation. But the International Conference straightened him out, and he became the most subservient member of the Liberal party in this House, so subservient that the government selected him to make all these wild, flimsy, untrustworthy statements in respect to the route over which this great transcontinental line shall be built.

The hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Justice have dilated to a considerable extent upon the interest that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would have in this eastern section, or what I shall term the government section. I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate, but I have not yet found out wherein the Grand Trunk Railway Company will have one cent's worth of interest in this government section. I have yet to see how the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be able to haul one pound of freight or how they will run their trains east from Winnipeg over the government division. Let us take an instance. The hon. Minister of Justice pointed out the great advantage that would accrue to the Grand Trunk Railway Company from hauling freight over their line to North Bay. To-day, if the Grand Trunk Railway Company wish to ship any commodity to British Columbia, how is that commodity sent ? Does it go to North Bay ? By an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway, Winnipeg freight goes via North Bay but every pound of freight that originates along the line of the Grand Trunk Railway for points in British Columbia travels from Chicago to Minneapolis and St. Paul and thence passes over the Great Northern Railway and is delivered at points in British Columbia. Let us suppose that the government division is constructed and let us suppose that the western division, or the Grand Trunk Pacific part, is also constructed. Would it be in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railwav Company to send their freight by way of North Bay and over the government line to Mr. FOWLER.
Winnipeg, or would it be in their interest to send it by way of Chicago ? By one route they would have their share of the freight right up to the city of Winnipeg, while by the other all they would have would be their share of the freight to North Bay, whatever it might be. Therefore, it is in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway to use their American line and the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not made up of children if this government is. The Grand Trunk Railway Company will use that connection and rightly so. I entirely endorse their action in so doing. The Grand Trunk Railway have no interest to east of Winnipeg in this new line. The only interest they will have in the so-called transcontinental railway will be the 25 per cent guarantee of the bonds for the construction of the road west of Winnipeg. In order to get a return on the bonds it has guaranteed on the western division would it not be in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway to take all the freight they could over the American line and across the continent from Winnipeg west over the Grand Trunk Pacific line thus adding to its earning power, first by helping the old portion of their system in Canada and in the second place by helping the subsidiary company between Winnipeg and the Pacific ocean ? I would be very pleased if the so-called expert would attempt to point out whereby the Grand Trunk Railway will ever haul one pound of freight over the line from Winnipeg to the east. If it is going to the sea-board does the Grand Trunk Railway touch it ? Never. Freight going from Winnipeg to the sea-board passes entirely over the government line leased by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway will not profit by the hauling of freight to the extent of a farthing. It touches Quebec and takes to the sea there, or goes down to the maritime provinces, it does not touch one mile of the Grand Trunk Railway. How can the Grand Trunk Railway be interested in that part of the business ? When the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Justice stand up and tell us about a verbal promise we might as well accept the promise of a boot-black on a pullman car as to accept such irresponsible promises as these. The Grand Trunk Railway Company will never haul a car of freight from Winnipeg to Quebec. The only advantage that they would have would be to haul it over their own line, because I expect that the government will not require the Grand Trunk Railway to use a Canadian Labe Superior port. The Grand Trunk Railway are entitled to use their American line for their eastern freight and they are not entitled to be forced north of the lakes in any sense whatever. If the government want to benefit Canada let them either control that northern line themselves or let them give a guarantee of bonds to some other company under an agreement, as the Manitoba government have done, so

that the Prime Minister could raise his hand and say : Rates shall come down. We have an example of that in the province of Manitoba. The premier of that province a year ago said :	Gentlemen of the Canadian Northern Railway, I want you to reduce your rate from 14 cents to 12 cents per bushel to Port Arthur. They kicked about it, but it was on the face of the agreement and the rate came down. There was no commission or Railway Committee of the Privy Council to state whether it should come down or not. This year Premier Rob-lin said to the Canadian Northern Railway : Gentlemen, we want that rate reduced to 10 cents under your agreement. The rate has come down and the farmers have the benefit of it. I want to tell the right lion. Prime Minister that if he in his wisdom wants to give the Grand Trunk Railway a British Columbia route by way of Chicago and Minneapolis from Winnipeg and through the Yellow Head or Pine River Pass I will not object. Let him come out and say so-and let him not pretend that we were going to have a Canadian end to it. Let him run the eastern section as a government institution and continue it through to the coast if he likes or let him give a guarantee of bonds to some) other company and then make an agreement by which he shall be able to control the freight rates on this portion of the road which will give us a Canadian route and whfch will bring about actual results which will never be brought about except in theory by the present scheme.

I would like to bring one or two matters in connection with this subject to the attention of the government again. In the first place it has been suggested that because this contract is attached to the proposed Bill we cannot make any amendment in it. Technically this is the case. Practically it is not so. A similar agreement was introduced for which ratification was asked in connection with a railway in the Yukon some years ago. That agreement was amended in at least one respect and I think in more than one respect before the measure passed this House. Parliament; declined to give its assent to the agreement in the form in which it came before the House and all difficulty in that regard was removed by the making of a supplementary agreement which was entered into by the government on the one hand and by the other parties to the contract on the other hand. We are not, I suppose, dealing with this matter as a mere matter of form. Parliament is not asked to discuss this with the idea that in the end it should go through in exactly the form in which it is presented. We are supposed to be doing some work in regard to this contract. We have already amended it by the assent of the government in what I think is a very important respect. The suggestion of my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) that we are haggling with
this matter, I can only excuse on the ground that he was not in the House when the government this morning accepted one of the amendments which I had the honour to propose.
He does not care anyway.

There is not the slightest objection to the Grand Trunk Railway going into the west. I myself have suggested in this House that the Grand Trunk Railway should have an opportunity of making connections between its system in Quebec and Ontario, and that great western country, and that every facility should be given to it for that purpose. We would be 'delighted to have the Grand Trunk Railway go into that country to develop it as far as possible, and we have no objection that they should even go in under the name of another corporation, as they are doing in the present case ; but when that other corporation is getting assistance from the government; when the Grand Trunk Railway is occupying the exceptionally favourable position of controlling the new proposed railway in the west, and receiving government aid for its construction, let us see that any stipulations that parliament in its wisdom may see fit to enact, shall be binding not only upon the nominal party to the agreement, but upon the real party to the agreement as well. Let us look at the attitude of the government with regard to this matter. In this contract; and I refer only to sections 42 and 43, in order to be brief, there is this stipulation, having reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific :
The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shippers, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through-rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time he greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that 'all such traffic not specifically routed otherwise by the shippers shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
What is the policy of the government with regard to that ? I am sorry the Prime Minister has left the House, because I would like to ask him this question :	Is It the
policy of the government, notwithstanding the aid that is being granted indirectly to the Grand Trunk Railway under this agreement, that the Grand Trunk Railway shall be absolutely at liberty to divert that traffic from Canadian ports. That is the way in which the agreement leaves the matter, and I challenge the Minister of Justice to deny my construction of this agreement in that regard. Is it the policy of the government that the Grand Trunk Railway, receiving this aid from the government in the form of subsidies and guarantees to the Grand Trunk Pacific, shall be fully at liberty to divert this traffic

from Canadian routes and from Canadian ports ? If that is the policy of the government, it is not our policy. I am putting before the House an amendment which is designed to impose upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company, all the obligations contained in the stipulations of that contract, and gentlemen on the treasury benches say they are not prepared to accept that proposition. When they take that course, they are simply declaring that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, to which this aid is really being given, shall be absolutely and fully at liberty to divert this traffic from Canadian routes and from Canadian ports. Is there any answer to that ? If there is, then during this debate of three or four hours I have not heard the answer, and I would like to hear it before the debate closes. In view of the action of the government upon this amendment, I assert that it must be the policy of the government, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, which is really receiving this aid from the government under the name of Grand Trunk Pacific, shall be absolutely at liberty to do tlie things which are forbidden to the nominal company by sections- 42 and 43 of that contract. What answer have the ministers to give to that ? Does the Minister of Justice say that the Grand Trunk Railway Company-not being a party to his contract, not being bound by any of its stipulations-is not absolutely at liberty to do what I have said ? This agreement, according to its recital, declares :
Whereas, having regard to the growth of population and .the rapid development of the production and trade of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and to the great area of fertile and productive land in all the provinces and territories as yet without railway facilities, and to the rapidly expanding trade and commerce of the Dominion, it is in the interest of Canada that a line of railway, designed to secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada and the provinces and territories west of the great lakes, to open up and develop the northern zone of the Dominion, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada, and to develop commerce through Canadian ports, should be constructed and operated as a common railway across the Dominion, from ocean to ocean, and wholly within Canadian territory.
That is the recital of the agreement and the recital of the Bill declares that a necessity has arisen for the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, to be operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion of Canada from ocean to ocean. Is there any danger point which we can suggest on the line of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is the real company, as the Minister of Finance lias himself declared more than once. I have already pointed out the great danger which the Minister of Trade and Commerce lias brought to the attention of tlie country, and I have shown that neither in his speech nor in any remarks which have been addressed Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
to us from tlie other side of the House, can we find that the slightest safe-guard has been provided against that very great danger. Where is the danger to be apprehended. In the first places in so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned, it is to be apprehended in respect to traffic gathered in the west and brought to the shores of Bake Superior. It is to be apprehended with respect to the traffic that is taken to the shores of the Georgian bay and delivered to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is at perfect liberty to carry it to Portland, notwithstanding anything in this agreement. Will any of the ministers now say that they can gainsay my statement in this respect ? They will not say so. We are asking to put in this contract a stipulation by the Grand Trunk Railway Company with regard to that very traffic, and tlie government say : It is not part of our policy that that trade should he sent through Canadian channels ; it is part of our policy that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, receiving this aid from the government, shall be perfectly at liberty to divert it to an American port. In the second place, is there any danger with respect to traffic brought over the eastern division of this proposed transcontinental railway ? Can it he taken to Portland instead of Halifax or St. John ? I cannot myself see why it should be brought over the eastern division when it can be brought to the shores of the Georgian bay and delivered to tlie Grand Trunk Railway there ; but let us assume that it can be brought over the eastern division to Montreal or to Quebec, at a time when navigation is closed at these ports. What will be the danger then ? The danger will be, that whereas the distance from Quebec to Portland is 318 miles by the Grand Trunk, and the distance from Montreal to Portland is 291 miles by the Grand Trunk ; the distance from Quebec to St. John-even by the short line proposed by this government -will he in the vicinity of 489 miles, or perhaps 460, if you construct a line from Chip-man ; and the distance to Halifax will he 586 miles. In giving these distances I adopt for the purpose the estimate of the Minister of IHnanee which I believe to be altogether too low. After that freight has been brought to Montreal or Quebec, what is to prevent the Grand Trunk Railway Company from carrying it over that shorter distance to its own terminals at Portland, which is open for navigation throughout the entire winter ?
There is nothing in this agreement which prevents that being done, and we are asking that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall enter into a stipulation that the traffic gathered in the west and brought over the eastern division of this transcontinental highway, shall not be diverted by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to United States ports hut shall be carried to Canadian ports

for export to Europe. The policy of the government is not to insert in the contract any stipulation of that kind. The policy of the government is to leave it absolutely and completely within the power of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to do the very thing I am suggesting; and for that reason they decline to insert in this Bill the proposed amendment. Let it be perfectly and distinctly understood what the issue between the two parties is. We on this side of the House say that if the Grand Trunk Railway Company gets this aid by means of the nominal company which has been created, the Grand Trunk Pacific, which it shall absolutely control, the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself should be subject to the stipulation which requires that traffic shall not be diverted from Canadian ports. The hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, for some reason which is best known to themselves, decline to accept that proposition, and say, although we put into this contract a stipulation which is binding on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, we shut our eyes to the greater danger of diversion of traffic by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and decline to insert any stipulation which shall impose a stipulation on the Grand Trunk Railway Company in that regard. There is another danger point which might be mentioned, and that is this. Suppose this traffic is brought in the winter time by the Grand Trunk Railway as far as North Bay or Gravenhurst by the branch lines which are to be constructed, what is there to prevent the Grand Trunk at these points taking the traffic on its own line to Portland instead of to St. John or Halifax ; is there a single stipulation in this contract which does not leave the Grand Trunk Railway Company absolutely and fully at liberty to do the very thing which I have suggested ? If this is the policy of the government-and it is their policy because they decline to accede to the amendment which I have suggested-it is just as well that the House should understand it, and that the country as a whole should understand it. It is just as well that the country should realize that although we have high-sounding words, although this enterprise is called a national transcontinental railway, and although the object of this Bill and of this agreement is stated to be the transportation of Canadian traffic along Canadian routes and to Canadian ports, nevertheless the government, for some reason which they do not see fit to explain to the House, are absolutely determined that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, from which the greatest danger in that regard is to be apprehended, shall be absolutely and fully at liberty to do the very thing which is recognized on all hands as a detriment to the development of our Canadian trade. Under these circumstances, it does not seem to me that any adequate defence has been made of the proposition of the government
in this regard. Does or does not the government regard as of any serious import the danger which has been pointed out by one of the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, the Minister of Trade and Commerce ? If that is regarded as a serious danger, is it not a danger to which this country shall be open the very day after this agreement is signed ? What possible reason can there be for refusing to insert in this Bill a provision by which the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in respect to the diversion of traffic at least, shall be subject to exactly the same restrictions, the same stipulations and the same covenants to which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the nominal party, is rendered subject by the terms of this agreement ?

With regard to the new point which my hon. friend has imported into the discussion, that is to say, the guarantees for the carrying of the traffic to the maritime provinces, we shall have to leave my hon. friend's remarks to go to some extent unanswered, because they deal with a part of the question which has been repeatedly discussed throughout the debate.
Will my hon. friend pardon me ? I do not think I raised any new point. I endeavoured to make it plain that I had made this point when I addressed the House a week ago.

It was a new point at this particular moment, though it is one which at earlier stages of this debate has been very fully discussed. What I imagine is the difficulty is this.
