Now, with regard to the question of fuel. Wood has been used upon railways, and it can be used again, and it is as cheap and effective a fuel as coal. But there is the chance of getting enormous quantities of peat in that region. It is a region amply supplied with peat, and peat widely distributed. I am told by those familiar with the preparation of peat that there is a process in use in Germany by which peat is prepared for fuel and furnishes the most excellent fuel for steam generating and domestic purposes, and moveover that the byproducts saved in preparing the peat pay for the expense of preparing it. If we have no other fuel supply we can use the peat located along the line of railway. The ingenuity of man will provide the means for using this material, so we need not trouble ourselves on that score. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) says there can never be local traffic there.

Never.
Ml*. CHARLTON. There are a good many predictions and prophecies made with regard to this road. If some of those who indulge in them live for a few years longer, they will be convinced they are neither prophets nor the sons of prophets. The country through which this road passes will develop a local trade in the products of the forest and the products of the soil. There is a line of railway from Sudbury to Port Arthur, 555 miles in length, which my hon. friend proposes to buy, if his scheme is adopted-the lean portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has no considerable local trade and never will have, for there is nothing to create it, neither timber nor soil. That is an entirely different country from the country through which this road will run. This is not Laurentian rock, it is not a stretch of granite as it is from Sudbury to Port Arthur ; it is not like that, a country of heavy tunnels, deep cuttings and steep grades, but a fruitful country, a country fit for settlement, a country well timbered, and a country that will create in due time, a vast local trade for the railway passing through it. The hon. gentleman says that nobody will go to that country as long as they can go to the prairies of the Nbrtli-west. But the fact is that the people are going to just such a country. All you need in order to get people into such a country, is to give them means of communication. The hardy pioneer, the axeman, the lumberman, will go there. And let me tell the hon. gentleman-for I have worked at the business of chopping down trees, logging up and clearing forest lands-that the hardy pioneer with his axe, a little food and a yoke of oxen will go to the woods, and will make headway, will make a farm and will acquire a competence with less capital than it requires to start on the prairies-very much less. If an man goes to the prairies, he must have money to buy lumber for a house,
to buy lumber for the barn, to buy lumber or wire and posts for fences. Everything he does in the way of putting up buildings or fencing his lands costs an outlay in money, but, if he goes to the forest, he builds his house of logs1, he can hew logs for the floor, he can rive out shingles for the roof. 1-Ie need spend no money, except for glass and nails. He can chop down the forest and he can put in the fire in the spring and burn off the brush, log up the logs and burn them, bring the land into cultivation and raise fine crops-and he cau do all this practically without capital. He has to endure hardships, it is true. He is a hero. But, in time, he has acquired a farm, be is surrounded with all the comforts of civilization, he has a competence, he is a man of means. Why, the hon. gentleman knows nothing of what he is talking about. There is a class of people who prefer that kind of country, and by this class of people the country will be settled. They are the hardiest and best element in the population of Canada-selfreliant, vigorous, frugal and patriotic. They will go into that country and will make a local business for this road-don't trouble your mind about that.	,
The hon. gentleman says that this road will only have four months' business out of the twelve. That will be unfortunate. Why, Sir, this road will have local business to the extent that it is created throughout the year. This road will have a business of transporting crops in all seasons from the west of the sea-board. It will have the advantage of taking grain, for instance, in the Peace river valley and putting it into Quebec on board vessels in nine days from the time it is loaded on the cars, less than half the time by which we can get i!t (to the sea-board by| any other route. That is an enormous advantage, the advantage of saving time. It can transport wheat to Quebec from the time of threshing until late in the autumn, and then it can keep transporting it to Halifax and St. John, until the next spring, when it can resume transporting it to Quebec. It is not going to be necessary to put that wheat all into the market within four or five months, for the country will develop in such a w:ay that there will be capital to carry the crops, and elevators to hold them ; and the busin-ness will be distributed over the year instead of the grain being rushed out to market in a few months, as is now done because the lakes close up and there is no communication. These are conditions in the transportation problem which need to be considered. These lions in the path, these bugaboos which our friends opposite conjure us, are difficulties only iri appearance and not in reality. These lion, gentlemen wish to impress the country with the idea that this is a bad measure. They ask the people to put them in power and they will buy roads already built ; they wiil take over 555 miles of road through the

rocks and put the country's money into that ; they will double-track roads from the lakes into" the North-west ; they will spend $150,000,000 and will not put $20,000,000 into new works. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, we have a good thing. We have adopted, in this transcontinental scheme, a plan that is in the interest of Canada, that is calculated to develop Canada, that is for the benefit of all Canada and of all classes of the people, a scheme that ought to command the support of every man in this House and every man in this country. I feel thus deeply with reference to this scheme, and I am sorry to see so many arguments used against it which, I believe, in many cases are entirely unfounded.

I would like to read the paragraph in the speech of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) which the hon. member got up to read. This speech was delivered on the 6th of May last, and the part that I shall quote is reported at page 3463 of ' Hansard.' The hon. gentleman took up the book but failed to read :
So when you reach Buffalo, it the competition Is keen, it the American railway lines find it necessary, in order to secure the control of the business of carrying wheat from Buffalo to New York at a price which would leave them a bare profit, iit can be done. I am told, on the New York Central Railway at fifty cents a ton, or one cent and six mills per bushel. So you have the possibility of carrying wheat from Port Arthur to New York for three cen:s a bushel, or at most four cents- a bushel. Now there are conditions which render it, in my opinion, impossible at present to compete with that route. It is useless to think of hauling wheat from a point as far west as Port Arthur by an all-rail route to Quebec or to Halifax at prices such as those I quoted with regard to the American lines.

As we are having the diversion of reading my speech of the 12th of May last and as some of it is read in the way the old Scotch woman repeated the eighth commandment ' though shalt steal' leaving out an essential part of it-I may read a portion of this speech and 1 will only say that in that speech I was proceeding upon the assumption that this road, if built, would be a road of the character of those we have now, and I was making my calculations upon the basis of the then existing transportation methods and facilities. I took in that speech broad ground in favour of a line from Quebec to Winnipeg, and I asserted, as the hon. gentleman says, that it had been stated that wheat could be hauled from Buffalo to New York for 50 cents a ton, and that would be the bare cost of hauling wheat without a profit or any allowance for bringing empties back. In the calculation I have made to-night with reference to these rates from Winnipeg east, I have shown what the actual rates charged upon these roads are, and what they have been. These quotations that the hon. gen-Mr. CHARLTON.
tlemen make of that speech are entirely foreign to the case, and utterly' irrelevant and childish in view of the purpose for which they are made.

It is curious to see how hon. gentlemen, when they are cornered in their statements and their assertions, will try to squeeze out of them. Now I want to draw the attention of this House to the scheme, and to the statements upon which they are going to spend $100,000,000 on that railway. We have had the whole scheme from the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) this evening, and his statements in support of it are so contrary to his previous statements that I know the country will have no confidence in them. I cannot understand why' the government will allow themselves to be so misled by the hon. gentleman as to believe that grain can be hauled by railway at any such rates as he has stated. He was so completely upset by the reply made by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), that I do not wonder at the lamentable spectacle he has given us to-uiglit. The building of a railroad is not such an extraordinary thing. We can get the opinions of engineers, we can have that whole country surveyed in a year, and all we ask the government to do, all the country wants them to do, is to delay proceeding with the construction of this road. The talk about there being no time to wait, and all that sort of thing, is completely played out now. We all know that we can wait. There is no difficulty about the bonding privilege, we are not going 'to be attacked by the United States. There is no reason why this government should not even now, at this late date, revise their scheme. We are only asking them to do what the whole country wants them to do ; and we are prepared on this side of the House, if they can bring forward a scheme with some data to back it, and to show that it is feasible, we will be only too glad to join with them in building the road. After a great deal of labour these mountains of information have got here, and we find that they are not even in the shape of a ridiculous mouse. The information, in fact tells against the government scheme. You turn it over, page after page, and you get information contradicting the statements that are made in this House about the richness of that country, about the magnificent forests, about the enormous amount of red and white pine. Hon. gentlemen must remember that in making statements of that kind they are going to he found out. If it turns out to be a fact that the timber is there, why not tell us all about it, and then we can go into the scheme with our eyes open.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to make an appeal to the government. I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not in the House, because I believe that he approached this subject with a heartfelt desire to do what he

thought was good for this country. But evidently he was urged into it. I did not know at that time that the hon. member for North Norfolk was so filled up with this subject himself. Indeed he was so full of it that he was rather reckless in making supposititious cases as to the grain that could be drawn over it. There is no absolute information about it. As ordinary business men, leaving politics out of tile question, if any one came to you with a project of that kind, and asked you to invest your money in it, there is not one of you would do it. I think the hon. member for North Norfolk would be grand at writing a prospectus for a shady company. He speaks of timber limits, and soil that produces potatoes being so rich-really, if it was not so serious it would be laughable. I can assure these gentlemen that the country is asking for information. What we have got is so limited, is so uncertain, is so unreliable, that I do hope the government will consent to the delay that we are asking for. I am not talking for the sake of talking, for the sake of smothering a railway scheme that is going to do good to the North-west. I am as much in favour of doing good to the North-west as any hon. gentleman opposite. But I say the scheme propounded by the leader of the opposition is one that will give the immediate relief that the Northwest wants a great. deal sooner than the scheme of the government, and at enormously less expense. If you want to bring your grain down to be shipped from Quebec or from Halifax the scheme of the leader of tlie opposition will do it. The hon. member for North Norfolk spoke about bringing grain by the carload from the Peace riper country. I do not believe that it will ever be brought from the Peace river country to the east. That grain will find its way westward to the Pacific ocean, and will be shipped to China and Japan in the shape of flour or foodstuffs. Millions and millions of the products of flour will go in that direction. it will pay better to take it there, because the haul will he shorter, and you will get a bettor price for it. There is no use in talking about bringing grain from the Peace river country to Quebec to be shipped, it can't be done. The furthest west you can go for grain will be Edmonton, and from Edmonton you can lay it down cheaper by taking it to Lake Superior and thence eastward. The hon. member for North Norfolk obtained his information from the authorities lie mentioned by not asking them exactly what he wanted. Had those authorities known that he wished to send 2,000 tons on each train, they would have given him a very different estimate. Estimating a 12-car train at the same price as a 43 or a 60-car train, you can see at once how ridiculous his statement is. Therefore, I would advise the government to consult other authorities in this matter, to consult with their own friends of the Grand
Trunk, and get their consent to withdraw this Bill until another session.

The figures that have been given to us to-night by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) have upset all previous notions about railway traffic. The difference between the calculations made by the horn member for North Norfolk as to what grain can be carried for and will be carried for on this new transcontinental railway, and what it is now carried for on other roads is so great that I must come to the conclusion that the hon. gentleman has made some terrible mistake in his calculations. If the hon. gentleman has not made a mistake in his calculations, surely the Grand Trunk Railway Company has been bleeding the farmers and grain dealers of this country white, as the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) Used to tell us about the national policy-in fact, worse than bleeding them white. I can scarcely think that the Grand Trunk Railway will thank the hon. member for North Norfolk for the expose he has made to-night of the apparent extortion that is being practised on the people of this country by that company. I propose to make a few comparisons, and I will leave it to the judgment of lmn. members of this House to say whether this statement of the hon. gentleman is reasonably within the mark or not, because if it is I must repeat what I said before that the Grand Trunk Railway Company and other railways have certainly been taking extortionate rates from the farmers for carrying grain, far beyond what I think any man had any preconceived notion of. Take the Grand Trunk Railway from the port of Oakville, in the county I have the honour to represent, in the matter of freight. I do not apprehend that it will be possible for this transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec to get a road of better grades than you will get from Oakville to Montreal, down the shore of Lake Ontario, and down the St. Lawrence river, where there is a decline, not a rise, in the road-bed, and consequently we cannot expect to find any grade even as great as that which the liom gentleman speaks of. We are told that this new road is to be modelled on the Grand Trunk Railway from Toronto to Montreal, that it is to be a road equally as good. There is no demand that it should be any better. Now, assuming-and I think I am quite within the mark when I do assume-that the grades on the Grand Trunk Railway from the county of Halton to Montreal are as light as any grades that can possibly be obtained on this new transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, I think this comparison will be a very fair one. I am very sorry that the hon. gentleman is leaving the Chamber, because I would like him to give an explanation of the figures which I propose to give. From Oakville to Mont-

real tlie distance is 354 miles, and the charge of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for carrying wheat is 7'20 cents pea- bushel. According to the calculation made 'by the hon. gentleman of .$1. with 50 cents added per train mile, the Grand Trunk Railway Company should at the present time carry grain from Oakville to Montreal for ITS cents per bushel.
What do they charge ?

They charge 7:20 cents, or they are charging 6 2 cents more than what the hon. gentleman tells us grain will be carried for from Winnipeg to Quebec over the new transcontinental railway. I would ask the hon. gentleman if that is not a fair comparison ? I will apply the same calculation to Brampton, which is 354 miles from Montreal. The present cost of carrying grain from Brampton to Montreal by the Grand Trunk Railway is 7 20 cents. The actual cost of carrying it, according to the hon. gentleman's calculation, basing it on the same rates as he says wheat will he carried from Winnipeg to Quebec, is 118 cents per bushel, or again an excessive rate of 6:2 cents per bushel which the Grand Trunk Railway Company are at present charging the people of Brampton, in Peel, represented by my hon. friend to my left (Mr. Blain), more than they should charge, or 500 pt?t cent more than would be a legitimate charge. I will take another place. From Collingwood to Montreal the distance is 402 miles ,and the cost of carrying wheat is 8-40 cents. According to the calculation of the hon. gentleman ns to the rate at which wheat can be carried from Winnipeg to Quebec, the Grand Trunk Railway Company should carry wheat from Collingwood to Montreal for 1'34 cents, ot they are charging 7'6 cents more than they are entitled to charge. Take it from Peterborough, and surely the grade from Peterborough to Montreal, on the Grand Trunk Railway, is as low a grade as possibly can be found on a line crossing the height of land nine times between Winnipeg and Quebec. The distance between Peterborough and Montreal is 286 miles. The Grand Trunk Railway, and no doubt the Canadian Pacific Railway also, charge 6 cents pet bushel. The rate at which the hon. gentleman tells us wheat can be carried for that distance over this new road will be less than 1 cent, or -95 of 1-cent per bushel, showing us that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway are actually charging the farmers and grain dealers of Peterborough 5'05 cents per bushel more for carrying grain than the same grain could be carried for over this new transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, or they are getting 500 per cent more than they are entitled to. We will take Midland, which is 388 miles from Montreal. The charge is 8'40 cents pet bushel. According to the hon. gentleman, * Mr. HENDERSON,
this grain ought to be carried from Midland to Montreal for 1-30 cents per bushel, showing, therefore, that the Grand Trunk Railway to-day according to his calculations, are charging the farmers around Midland and the grain dealers of Midland 7TO cents per bushel more to carry the grain from Midland to Montreal than ought to be charged, according to the rate that the hon. gentleman has given us for the carrying of grain from Winnipeg to Quebec. Now, I think it is not necessary to do more than to point out these figures to show the absolute absurdity of the calculations made by the hon. gentleman. I cannot understand how he can reconcile his figures with the actual charges at the present time. To my mind, something ought to be done in regard to rates, both on the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, if these enormous charges are being extorted from the people over and above what a fair paying rate would mean. The only fair conclusion I can arrive at is that the hon. gentleman has made, as my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has pointed out, some terrible blunder in his calculations, and that they are utterly unreliable. No confidence whatever can be reposed in them, and I hope and trust that the government will not base their conclusion as to the transcontinental railway, whether they will go on with this transcontinental railway or defer it for another year, on such erroneous calculations as we have had from their expert to-night.

Mr. Chairman, I think that a careful study of the figures given by the h*n. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) will show that he has made some miscalculation in his figures in some directions. The greater part of the hon. gentleman's speech was based on the calculation, that a trainload should consist of 2,000 tons. He quoted the authority of Mr. Scott of the Great Northern, that a train would consist of forty-five cars, each car carrying 1,000 bushels, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) went on to calculate, that such a train woidd consist of 2,000 tons of freight, but in reality such train contains ony 1,323 tons, or two-thirds of two thousand tons. To commence with, the figures of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) are incorrect to the extent of one-third. Then the hon. gentleman referred very frequently to information he is in possession of, derived from the engineers who are now engaged in locating the route for the proposed transcontinental railway. If there is such information in possession of gentlemen on the government side, gentlemen on this side of the House should be supplied with it as well.

I stated that I got this information from the engineer of the Great Northern Railway. It is not information of an official character. I met that gentleman with Mr. Scott on Friday, and I received this

information from him, which I assume is correct.
That is as to the work of the surveying parties.
Yes, he had control of the surveying parties of the Trans-Canada, and I think he was in communication with the Grand Trunk.
It is unfortunate that we on this side of the House are not in possession of that report.
You have it in the same way as I got it, except that I am the intermediary.

I have heard several times about the corridors that the government was in receipt of information from parties in the field, and I think that has been stated in the House by others than the hon. member (Mr. Charlton). If the government have such information, it is important that it should be laid on the Table so that all members of the House may have the advantage of it in discussing this question. It must bo remembered however, that the Trans-Canada surveys passed a very great distance from the proposed route for the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Trans-Oanada passed north of Lake Winnipeg or about 300 miles from the city of Winnipeg. I have always understood that their line was to pass at one point about 100 miles south of James bay, which is about 150 miles north of the propose! route for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the information obtained for the Trans-Oanada would therefore have no relation whatever to what the gradients may be on the Grand Trunk Pacific. If there be any country easy for railway construction, it will probably be found in the alluvial plain which occurs at the foot of James bay, and which is referred to by Dr. Robert Bell as being a comparatively narrow basin inclosed within a circular rampart of rocks, and which circular rampart approaches at its northern terminus,where it flanks James bay east and west forming the eastern and western boundaries of that alluvial basin, which there is in the neighbourhood of 200 miles in diameter. Therefore, the alluvial tract, which has been referred to frequently as being in the neighbourhood of James bay, is bounded on each side by considerable obstacles in the form of a great drop in the land, which gives rise to a number of waterfalls, which are referred to in all the reports, and which have been spoken of in the course of this debate as likely to furnish opportunity for developing a great deal of water power. That being the case, we are not in possession of such information as would warrant us in concluding that the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) is right in assuming, that it is a certainty that a railway line -can be laid down in that country, which would give a maximum grade of four-tenths of one per cent a mile. Upon that supposition the 374
argument of the hon. gentleman rests, and if that cannot be realized, then all the figures he has used here with a grSat deal of skill, to prove that freight can be carried at these surprisingly low rates, absolutely lose their foundation.
Mr. CHARLTON, I did make a calculation of a six-tenths grade which was quite' satisfactory, but I also made a calculation on a four-tenths grade.

According to my knowledge, the Trans-Canada line was projected through the easiest and most level course that could be procured anywhere, and still the chief engineer, Mr. Doucet, only spoke to me of six-tenths grades, and I did not learn from him that it would be possible to realize anything better. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton has said that the engineers did not realize a better grade than six-tenths, because they did not look for it. It can searely be possible that they would not try to realize the very best possible grade, because the whole argument which was addressed by the promoters of the Trans-Canada to the government, to whom they were looking for a subsidy; and to the public, from whom they were seeking financial support; rests upon the fact that they hoped to secure a line which would furnish exceedingly easy gradients, and would enable them to carry timber into the west, and wheat from the west to Quebec, at a cheap rate.
The engineer said that while they found isix-tenths grade there would be no difficulty in finding four-tenths, only the cost would be increased somewhat; but it could be done quite easily.

Of course, by incurring greater expense in construction, easier grades could be procured. But the whole possibility of carrying freight at very low rates, such as have been cited by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton), would necessitate that it must be a comparatively cheap road to build. In all the calculations made by the hon. gentleman to-night, he has not taken into account anything which I think will be at all adequate to meet such fixed charges as would be necessary to secure a grade of four-tenths per cent. Such a road must be constructed at a very large cost. I think we must assume that the figures given by the Finance Minister of the estimated cost of this- road, $28,000 per mile, would not permit of any very extensive engineering works to secure such a grade in a country where there is any difficulty in getting such grades. The calculation that wheat can be carried from Winnipeg to Quebec for G cents and a fraction per bushel seems to me a very difficult one to maintain and even a more difficult one to believe, when we remember that that road from Winnipeg to Quebec, for over 400 miles, would run through the same country as the Canadian



Pacific Railway and the Central Northern Railway ; and under the pressure that can be brought to bear on these railroads by the local government of Manitoba, which as the result of making concessions to these railroads, has the power to extract the best possible terms from them, and in spite of all the other pressure which can be brought to bear by public opinion and every other agency, it has been impossible to reduce the cost of carrying grain from Winnipeg to Port William, a distance of something like 400 miles, below 8-4 cents per bushel.
That is from Brandon.

It includes Brandon points. And yet, the hon member for North Norfolk asks this House to believe that this new road will carry grain from Winnipeg, past Fort William, across Ontario, and across Quebec to the city of Quebec, three times the distance, for three-fourths of the cost. It is an immense assumption ; and it would require absolute demonstration to warrant any person whatever in believing it possible, especially when it is recollected that the House is approaching the consideration of this subject without very much information of a positively certain character. I say that to ask the House to decide on a question that involves such an amazing assumption is to ask too much.

Perhaps I might, in candour and fairness at this stage, if my hon. friend would permit me, say that we want to deal with this question in view of all the facts. In my calculations I distinctly confined myself to the cost of moving grain, basing them on a train mileage cost, which includes all the expenses of the road ; but I said that this train mileage cost would not include the interest on the investment in the road. That is something that has to be taken into consideration, and that would necessarily increase the price to be charged for the transaction of the business. My hon. friend deals .with the question as if there were no such element in the matter, and it may be that the cost is lower than it would be, because that element has to be taken into consideration.

I may have been doing an injustice to the hon gentleman ; but I was taking his figures to be, as I thought he intended them to be, based on his assumed estimate of $1 per train mile of the cost, and on the further assumption that trains could carry 2,000 tons. So far as the Lake St. John road is concerned, I have shown that the case cited by Mr. Scott did not provide for a train of 2,000 tons, but only 1,300 tons. As to the fixed charges and the interest charges on that road, they would have this effect, that after it goes into operation, and has secured so much of the wheat traffic of the west as to get even 30,000,000 bushels of grain to carry out in one year, that is to say, three-fourths of the wheat shipped from Winnipeg last year, if
the figures given by the hon. member for North Norfolk are correct, the total earnings of the road for all that enormous traffic would only realize $900,000 of gross earnings, whereas the interest the company would have to pay to the government of Canada on the cost of the road would amount to practically $1,500,000 ; so that unless it could succeed in developing some large and remunerative source of revenue, from which it cannot be understood to	come at this moment, the
road, after carrying the whpat. would be left short $60,000 to pay the goviern-ment the interest on the cost of the road. However, it seems to me not necessary for the House to proceed too seriously to consider the argument of the hon. member for North Norfolk until he produces figures which are more easily verified, all his statements make such drafts on the credulity of the members of this House that when one comes to estimate the improbability of all these assumptions, one realizes that the whole argument is not deserving of really serious consideration. I do not know what it was that provoked the hon. gentleman to resume the consideration of this part of ihe railway problem, as I think it was undesirable at this time to pursue th,.. line of argument.
The Minister of Finance {Hon. Mr. Fielding) is very fond of using the expression that someone is guilty of drawing a red herring across the scent. Now, if I have ever seen a red herring drawn across the scent and very successfully drawn for a considerable time, it has been done this evening by the hon. member for North Norfolk. We were engaged in the discussion of a definite proposal, the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition which dealt very specifically with a definite proposition and I must admit that although I have always found the Minister of Finance very ingenious and ready to cope with atny argument, he satisfied me that he was unable to grapple^ with the arguments of the leader of the opposition at all, in fact he had no answer to make to them. He resurrected the very ancient matter of the compact made by the government of the late Sir John Macdonald with the Canadian Pacific Railway twenty years ago. At a critical moment the hon. member for North Norfolk {Mr. Charlton) came to; his rescue and introduced into the discussion considerations that were dealt with over a month ago, and for the last hour or more our attention has been diverted to problematical railway hauls and to an ideal railroad which I would like but do not expect to see realized. To come back to the subject which is really before the House I feel that the opposition cannot go too far in sustaining the position taken by their leader. His amendment asks the government for nothing more than is contained in the jjroposition submitted to the House by the government. According

to the present contract the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway undertakes to arrange or provide-and to a certain extent the whole contract is based on this-that the Grand Trunk Railway shall do certain things; that it shall stand behind the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway; that it shall finance that company and that it shall afterwards carry on the business of that company in so far as it can control that business, in such a manner as to secure to the people of Canada the full benefit of the road and all the advantages that should accrue from the large expenditure which Canada is asked to make. When the leader of the opposition, without going outside the terms of the contract, without suggesting any new proposition, asks the government to add to their Bill, words that will make it absolutely clear that the Grand Trunk Railway shall do the very thing which the contract implies it shall do, the government instead of complying with that reasonable proposition or advancing some reasons why they should not agree to it, fell back on the consideration of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance suggests a great many considerations and suggests them with great ingenuity but not one of them to my mind at all touches the subject. The leader of tbe opposition and the opposition are not asking for anything new; they are merely asking that the government shall add such words to their Bill as will guarantee that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall do and shall abstain from doing the very things which they tell us it is the purpose of the Bill that the Grand Trunk Railway shall do or abstain from doing. In answer to the very clearly proVteu case of the leader of the opposition in which he shows that the Grand Trunk Railway is everything in this contract and that the government has impressed on the House and on the country the idea that it is of the greatest importance to this country that the Grand Trunk Railway should be interested and should undertake some responsibilities in connection with this Bill, they still declined to view with favour the proposition of the leader of the opposi-tjon and to put such language into the Act as shall insure that the Grand Trunk Railway shall do those things which it is understood this contract implies they shall do. The leader of the opposition has pointed out that the Grand Trunk Railway is not directly bound and yet is to have absolute control in the future is to have the majority of the stock and is to be in a position to dictate the policy of the new road, to elect its directors, to frame its policy or change its policy, to rule it in every respect, as, when and how it pleases. I am not as dependent upon other people's brains as some hon. members of this House. The cost and facilities of transport of the export surplus, under certain circumstances, is the most important influence in fixing the value of the crop and the farmer's profit. Water transportation is cheaper than rail. If the Canadian wheat fields were on the shores of the great lakes, and if the lakes were open all the year round, there would be no need of a railway to carry the export surplus to ocean ports. But the eastern edge of the wheat fields is 400 miles west of the lakes, and the lakes are closed for five months in the year. During the whole year the wheat must reach the lakes by a rail haul of from 400 to 1,400 miles, and during nearly half the year it must go forward, to the ocean all rail, or await the following season of navigation. The season of lake navigation is the season during which the crop is sown and grown, and not more than two, or at the outside three months of navigation remain after harvest.
If crop which does not cross the lakes in the fall is held by the farmer awaiting lake transport next spring, the money value does not go into circulation, and the farmer himself and the business of the country suffer a loss which cannot be counted in cents per bushel. If it passes from the farmer to the dealer, it must pay the costs of storage for the winter and incidental expenses. The dealer must protect himself against the possibility of a lower market the following summer by a margin over the mere cost of storage, which may be called a commercial insurance. These conditions tend to throw the grain trade into the hands of a few strong companies, which means monopoly in buying, and. therefore, an illegitimate lowering of prices to the producer. The result is to reduce the fair profit of the farmer and to keep the grain trade and. all business dependent upon it in an unsettled and unsatisfactory condition, to the general disadvantage and loss of the whole country.

During the past two seasons not more than one-quarter of the crop reached the sea-board by the lake route without paying winter storage charges. As the crop acreage increases, the proportion which must stand winter storage charges or go forward ail rail must increase, unless the railway accommodation across the wheat fields andi to the lakes is increased proportionately. At best it is a physical impossibility for more than half an average crop to he taken across the lakes before the close of navigation. The summer rate by lake and rail, Brandon to Montreal, last year averaged 164 cents per bushel. The winter storage, insurance and other definite charges were 5 cents per bushel, making a total charge, Brandon to Montreal by lake and rail, on winter stored grain of 214 cents. Two million bushels of wheat were for-war-ded all rail, Brandon to St. John, last winter by the Canadian Pacific Railway, at the same average rate of 214 cents per bushel. But the all-rail shipments saved the margin required for commercial insurance, caught the highest market price, enabled business to be done on smaller capital and thereby cut out monopoly, shifted the grain trade from a speculative to a business basis, and demonstrated that an all-rail haul was a practical proposition.
Although a necessary charge, the margin taken by the dealer as a commercial insurance is not a fixed amount, and can only be approximately arrived at. Last season me dealers dropped from summer to winter prices on October 18th. From that date until a short time before the close of navigation, on December 6th, two prices were current at all purchasing points, one the elevator price, and the other the car price. The elevator price was the final market value, with the lake and rail transport, costs of winter storage, commercial insurance, &c., deducted. The car price was the same market value, with only the cost of summer transport deducted. At 181 purchasing points in the west, under observation of the grain commissioner, the spread between the two prices was from 7 to 94 cents per bushel. That is, over and above the storage charges of 5 cents, the buyers took from 2 cents to 44 cents a bushel for commercial insurance and incidentals. It is evident that the higher the fall price, the greater the chance of a drop before spring, and, therefore, the greater the margin for commercial insurance the buyer must take to protect himself, and so the greater the loss to the farmer. On a crop of 50,000,000 bushels, only half of which can go forward by water direct, the loss to the farmer on the remaining half, because of its being held in storage until spring instead of going forward all rail, at an average allowance of 3 cents per bushel for commercial insurance and incidentals, is three-quarters of a million dollars. On a crop of 50,000,000 bushels, of which only a fourth goes forward by water
direct, the loss will be over a million dollars. And, estimating a spread of 44 cents per bushel, the loss would be nearly a million and three-quarters. There is no means of arriving at the loss from not getting the wheat forward to meet rises in the market, but it may very well be greater than the charge for commercial insurance and all incidentals. The Canadian Pacific Railway have not encouraged the all-rail haul, because the road was not built to accommodate that trade; because they have not the equipment which it would require; but chiefly because it was easier and better for them, until forced by circumstances to take a high rate per mile for the short haul to Fort William than a low rate per mile for the long haul to St. John. The Canadian Pacific Railway line from Brandon to St. John is 2,035 miles long. It pays interest at 4 per cent on a capitalization of $64,700 a mile, or five and a quarter millions a year.
The proposed Grand Trunk Pacific, from a like prairie point will be 1,930 miles to St. John. It can only be capitalized for its cost, on which it pays 3 per cent interest. A-t $30,000 per mile, it will have to pay $1,440,000 a year, or less than a third of the fixed charges of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The road will be built according to modern railway requirements and operated by_ modern methods. Therefore, if the Canadian Pacific Railway can haul grain at all at the rate of last winter, the Grand Trunk Pacific can haul it profitably at the same, and possibly at a less rate.
The yearly congestion of the western grain trade is partly natural and partly artificial. The winter congestion is natural; the fall congestion is artificial. The artificial congestion may not occur at all, or it may last for one or two months in the fall. It can be remedied by an adequate increase of transportation facilities west of the lakes.
The natural congestion must occur, and must last for at least five, and practically for six months. Its only remedy is transport by an all-rail route to a winter port, on terms which will permit a rate based on the cost of construction and cost of haul. This is provided for by public ownership, the lowest rate of interest on actual coet. and government control of rates.

There is another amendment outstanding which the government asked time to consider. I beg leave to move that amendment as follows :
That section 7 be amended by adding thereto the following subsections :-
(2)	Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the said agreement contained, His Majesty the King acting in respect of the government of Canada shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry ouit or fulfil any of the covenants, undertakings, conditions or stipulations in the said agreement contained on behalf of His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have subscribed for the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company payable in cash at par to the amount of not less than $24,900,000.
(3)	The Grand Trunk Railway Company shall hold the said common stock to the amount aforesaid so subscribed for and acquired -is aforesaid, during the entire term of the lease mentioned in clause 20 of the said agreement, and so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government under .the terms of the said agreement shall remain outstanding and unpaid, and no pledge, transfer or conveyance of any part of the said stock during the said period shall be valid or effectual.
